activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
story:
The radio above the teller counter at Meridian Savings had been muttering all morning, and Raphael, restocking deposit slips at sixteen for minimum wage, caught only fragments until the word "Federal Reserve" surfaced through the static. The Fed had raised rates again. He stopped, a rubber-banded stack of slips in each hand, and turned to the nearest teller.

"Which rate does the Fed actually set?" he asked. "Like, my mortgage rate? I don't have a mortgage, but if I did."

She laughed without looking up from her screen. "Not your mortgage. The federal funds rate. That's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves."

"Banks lend to each other?" Raphael pictured men in suits passing envelopes across a dark parking lot.

"Every night, in huge amounts. Now go unjam the copier before Mr. Kaur sees it."

At lunch he texted Amar, who was doing a economics packet for summer school, and Flora, who read the news the way other people read horoscopes, fatally and daily. They showed up at four, occupying the lobby chairs meant for customers, looking, as Mr. Kaur observed drily, "like a lugubrious jury waiting to disenfranchise somebody." Flora took this as a compliment.

"Okay," Raphael said, pulling a chair into their huddle. "So the Fed raised this overnight rate. And everyone on the radio acts like it's a spell that fixes inflation. But it's just banks charging each other more to borrow for one night. How does that slow prices at the grocery store?"

Amar, who had the packet and therefore authority, spread it on his knees. "It says here higher rates discourage borrowing and spending."

"That's the textbook sentence. It doesn't say how the overnight part connects to anything. It's like saying exercise makes you healthy and never mentioning the heart."

Flora looked up from her phone. "My mom refinanced last year and the loan officer talked about the prime rate, which follows the Fed rate, and then their credit card went up two statements later. It's a chain. The overnight rate is the first link."

Raphael sat with that. A chain, not a spell. Each bank deciding, link by link, that money cost more this month than last, until the cost reached a bakery owner who delayed buying a second oven, until it reached a family that kept the old car another year. Nobody decreed the slowdown; it traveled. And the same chain that cooled prices could cool hiring, could cool Flora's mother's hours at the warehouse. The whole thing rested on a lever pulled in one building in Washington, and he understood, suddenly, both why his grandfather trusted it and why Flora called it "a machine for disenfranchising people who borrow." Both were partly right, which was the most irritating possible answer.

"But here's what I still don't get," he said aloud. "Nobody forces the banks to pass it along. They could just... not."

"They won't," Flora said, with the flat stoicism of someone whose predictions about institutions had a perfect losing record. "If borrowing from another bank costs more overnight, they'll charge everybody more. It's not generosity o'clock in banking."

"So it slows inflation by making everything more expensive first," Amar said slowly, writing this in the margin of his packet like a heresy he intended to keep. "That's a weird medicine."

"It's a medicine that works on the whole body, not the sick part," Raphael said, then winced. "Okay, that metaphor is doing too much. Forget the metaphor."

Mr. Kaur came over with the evening deposit bag and stood listening for a moment, which they noticed too late to pretend to be working. Raphael braced for a lecture, or worse, a compliment. Instead Mr. Kaur said only, "The copier is jammed again," and, walking away, "Tell Flora her mother's business account is fine." Flora exhaled.

What stayed unresolved, Raphael decided on the bus home, was everything worth asking. Whether slowing inflation was worth a year of scarier rent; whether the chain could ever be pointed at the people most able to bear it; whether a sixteen-year-old with rubber-banded deposit slips had any standing to ask. He took out his phone and started a note titled QUESTIONS THAT DON'T FIT IN MARGINS. The first line read: who decides which link pays. Below it he wrote the second, smaller: ask the teller about reserves tomorrow. The bus hissed to his stop, and he ran for it through the rain, the note still glowing in his hand.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
story:
Coralie set her laptop on the kitchen table between the fruit bowl and her mother's unread newspaper, and opened the spreadsheet she had started at eleven that morning. In column A she had listed the widths of rectangles under a curve, the curve being some ordinary parabola she had drawn herself, and in column B the sum of all the rectangle areas. With ten rectangles the total was 32.5. With a hundred it was 33.32. With ten thousand the number had stopped changing in the first four decimal places, sitting at 33.333 like a bird gone still on a wire.

The problem was that she did not believe it. That was the actual problem, more than the homework itself. Ms. Bekele had set only six integral exercises, due Monday, and Coralie had finished five of them in forty minutes by following the rules: reverse the power, add one to the exponent, divide. But the sixth asked her to explain, in a sentence, what the answer meant, and she had sat there realizing she could produce the number without being able to say what it was a number of. Her friend Payton would have written something confident and vague and gone to bed. Coralie had once watched Payton argue a full essay's worth of conviction out of one skimmed paragraph, and the whole class had lionized him for it, called him brilliant, and she had felt the small disincentive that comes from being the person who says, quietly, that she doesn't understand yet.

She remembered then her grandfather's workshop, the summer she was eleven. He had been fitting a shelf into an alcove that was not square, because the old house had settled unevenly over a century, and the alcove's back edge sloped. He could not measure the slant with one number. So he had cut thin wooden strips, maybe twenty of them, each standing upright against the sloping wall, each a hair taller than the last, and laid the shelf across their tops. It followed the curve, roughly. When she asked why he didn't just cut it right, he said the wall was crooked in a way no single cut could match, and that the shelf only had to rest on enough points to forget it was resting on strips at all.

Back at the table, she widened column C and typed a new set of widths. Ten rectangles: 32.5. Then she made them thinner, more of them, the same stretch of curve sliced into narrower and narrower slivers. She watched the totals creep together, the gap between overestimate and estimate narrowing each time, the whole column converging on 33.333 the way the shelf had settled onto the wall. She typed into her homework document: the sum of the rectangle areas gets closer and closer to one number as the rectangles get thinner.

Her phone buzzed. Everleigh, from two streets over: "are you still doing the bekele thing?? it's 11." Then a second message: "i just wrote that integration is when you find the area." Coralie looked at the words and felt the old fork in the road, the one between saying something true and saying something finished. She typed back, "area under the curve. and the number is the limit of the sums. the rectangles get infinitely thin." Then, before she could second-guess it, "come over tomorrow, i'll show you the spreadsheet."

She spent another while testing the idea against the curve she trusted least, one that dipped and rose, where the rectangles sat partly above and partly below the axis and she had to decide what to do with the pieces underneath. The sums still settled, though she was not sure she could defend every step of it. She left a note to herself in the margin of her notebook, a question mark beside the word "below," because she would rather bring Ms. Bekele the honest gap than the polished blank. Somewhere in the middle of this her mother came down in her robe, put the kettle on, and said nothing, only touched the top of Coralie's head on her way past, which in their house meant both goodnight and approval.

At the end she read her sentence again, then rewrote it: a Riemann sum approximates the area under a curve by adding up the areas of thin rectangles, and the integral is the limit as the rectangles become infinitely thin. It was almost the language of the textbook, but now it carried the shelf, the strips, the long afternoon of watching numbers settle. She closed the laptop halfway, the screen dimming to a wedge of light on the wood, and thought she could still see the column in her mind, all those thin gray bars standing shoulder to shoulder under the curve.

Everleigh texted once more, just "bring snacks." Coralie smiled, opened the laptop again, and copied the file to a second sheet titled for tomorrow, then sat looking at the last total, 33.333333, the threes going on past where the cell could hold them.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
The library's reading room had gone glacial by the time Rosalie spread her notes across the table, and she pulled her sweater sleeves down over her knuckles without looking up from the paperback. The Good Soldier, Ford Madox Ford, 1915. Her seminar teacher had assigned it with a warning she'd repeated twice: trust nothing the narrator tells you. Rosalie had underlined half the first page already, which she suspected was exactly wrong, like applauding a magician before the trick.

Zion dropped into the chair across from her and slid a coffee across the table, contraband under the no-drinks sign. "You've been in here since four. I saw your bike locked to the same post." He leaned over the book. "Is it actually sad, or is that just what the cover promises?"

"It opens with him saying, 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard.'" She tapped the line. "That's the whole first sentence, basically. John Dowell, the narrator."

"Heard it where? Somebody tell it to him at a bar?"

Rosalie opened her mouth and then stopped. She turned back to page one and read the sentence again, mouthing it this time. Because she had read the next hundred and fifty pages last night on her bed, flashcards of plot abandoned on the quilt, and Dowell had not heard the story. He had stood inside it. His wife, his best friend, the affair, the sanatorium, the whole slow ruin, and he was calling it something that had happened to other people, told to him secondhand over dinner.

"Zion," she said slowly, "he lived it. All of it. He's a character in it. And he says he heard it."

"So he's lying?" Zion looked pleased, the way he did when a book turned out to contain a crime.

"No." She was aware of Ms. Qureshi a few shelves away, reshelving returns with the quiet competence of someone who knew exactly what everyone at every table was doing and had decided to let them keep doing it. "Not exactly lying. It's more like..." She reached for it. "Like he's putting himself in the jury box instead of the witness stand. Like he wants the acquittal."

Zion raised an eyebrow at the word, and she waved him off.

There had been a moment last spring she kept returning to, the way you press a bruise. Kailyn had told her, in the hallway outside the gym, that a boy in their grade had said something about Rosalie at a party, and Kailyn had reported it in the third person, carefully, as though she'd only heard about the party too. Rosalie had later found out Kailyn had been standing right there. It had not been the betrayal itself that stung so much as the grammar of it, the way her friend had extenuated her own silence by narrating her own presence out of the sentence. Rosalie had never said she knew. She wasn't sure, even now, whether that made her generous or a coward.

"You're doing the face," Zion said.

"I'm thinking about point of view." She pulled her legal pad closer. "Okay, so here's my problem. My whole essay was going to be about how Dowell is a fool and Ford is laughing at him. But it's not that simple. If he says he heard the saddest story, and we know he lived it, then the sentence is doing two things at once. He's telling the truth about the sadness and lying about the distance, and the lie might be the only way he can carry the truth." Her pen hovered. "Or I've got it backwards. Maybe Ford wants us to catch it in the first sentence so we never relax again."

"So which is it?"

"I don't know yet." She said it plainly, and it felt less like defeat than like standing on solid ground.

Kailyn arrived at seven, cheeks red from the cold, peeling off her scarf. "Ms. Qureshi says you have the room reserved until closing and I'm to bring carbohydrates." She set down a bag of bagels. "What are we solving?"

Rosalie slid the book to the middle of the table, open to page one, and covered everything after the first line with her hand. "Read that," she said. "Just that. Out loud."

Kailyn read it, the saddest story she had ever heard, and frowned at it, and Rosalie watched her friend's eyes move backward through the sentence, hunting for the thing that was wrong with it, the way you retrace a staircase in the dark to find the missing step. Behind them, Ms. Qureshi pushed her cart past, paused, and said nothing, though the corner of her mouth suggested she had heard everything for the last hour.

"It says heard," Kailyn said at last. "But it's his story."

"Yeah," Rosalie said, and took the book back, and turned to page two. "Now watch what he does with the word normally."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
story:
Jacob's grandfather kept the radio tuned to a Spanish station even when he wasn't listening, so the kitchen filled with talk shows and cumbia while Jacob sat at the vinyl table with his note cards, trying to argue about water rights in a language he had studied for exactly three years. The assignment from Ms. Teo was simple and, to him, terrifying: five minutes, entirely in Spanish, on a current issue, no notes after the first sentence. He had chosen the city's drought restrictions because his grandfather had opinions about them, opinions delivered in rapid, unforgiving Spanish across the dinner table every night that week.

"You argue like a lawyer who lost his briefcase," his grandfather said on Tuesday, which Jacob took as encouragement, since on Monday the assessment had been worse.

Dana came over on Wednesday with her laptop and a bag of limes, and she set up on the porch while Jacob paced the flagstones reciting his opening. She was doing the same assignment in French, and they had agreed to be each other's hecklers, since the point, Ms. Teo had said, was not the smoothness of the sentences but the sturdiness of the thinking inside them. That was the part Jacob kept turning over. At school he could argue in English all day, quick and sharp, the kind of sharp that won lunchroom debates and lost nothing. In Spanish, all his speed abandoned him. He had to build each sentence like furniture, and while he built it, he could hear the flaw in the idea underneath.

"Try the part where you answer the other side," Dana said, squeezing a lime into her water. Jacob nodded and began, and his grandfather appeared at the screen door with a dish towel over his shoulder, saying nothing, which was his way of settling in.

Prince arrived on Thursday with his skateboard and no plans to leave. He spoke almost no Spanish, but he had watched enough debate clips online to have strong feelings about technique, and he sat on the porch rail while Jacob ran the full five minutes for the first time. Jacob's counterargument section was where he had planned his best move. The strongest argument against his own position, the one his classmate Marco would surely make at the actual debate, was that residential restrictions were pointless when agriculture used most of the water. Marco was also, famously, the son of a man who owned a car wash. Jacob had written a line about that, a joke at Marco's expense, and he delivered it now, waiting for the laugh.

Prince didn't laugh. "What does that even have to do with the farms?"

"It shows he's a hypocrite," Jacob said. "His dad wastes water all day."

"So? Is he wrong about the farms?"

Jacob opened his mouth and found nothing in it. His grandfather, still at the screen door, said a single word in English, which he almost never did. "Ad hominem." He dried a glass slowly. "Attacking the man instead of the claim. In formal debate, it is a fallacy." Then he went back inside, and the screen door clapped shut behind him as if it were grading the moment.

Jacob sat down on the steps. He had known the term existed somewhere, in some unit Ms. Teo had taught in the fall, but he had never felt it from the inside before, the seduction of it, how the joke had seemed like strength. The realization didn't deflate him; if anything, it invigorated him, because now he could see the actual shape of the argument, the real hinge where his evidence met Marco's, and it had nothing to do with anyone's father. He rewrote the section that afternoon at the kitchen table, the radio murmuring, and found that the slower language was doing something English never had for him: it made dishonesty physically difficult, a sentence he couldn't honestly support simply wouldn't come out.

On Friday evening Dana brought her French debate and he brought his Spanish one, and they performed for an audience of Prince, the grandfather, and Ms. Teo, who had been invited to dinner and arrived with a lemon cake like a neutral observer crossing a border. When Jacob reached the counterargument, he laid out Marco's position better than Marco ever had, gave it its full weight, and then answered it with the aquifer data, and when he stumbled on a verb he simply stopped, said "perdón," and kept going. The five minutes ended with him still standing, which felt like more than it probably was.

Afterward, on the porch, in the blue hour when the street went quiescent and even the dogs had given up barking, Prince asked him whether he'd won. Jacob said he didn't think that was the right question anymore, and then, because ennui was creeping in around the edges of the evening, the empty feeling after something you feared turns out to be survivable, he asked Dana whether she thought honesty was easier or harder in a language you owned less of.

"Both," she said, and handed him the last slice of cake.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
The signup table was a folding card table with a clipboard, and the clipboard had a coffee ring on it, and that was the whole apparatus of the neighborhood cleanup. Isabelle wrote her name under Felicia's, and Felicia leaned over and added a star next to both of them, and then Mr. Gupta, who ran the food bank warehouse behind the parking lot where they were picking up trash, handed them each a pair of gloves.

"Inside or outside," he said. "Your choice. Outside you get the sun. Inside you get the walk-in freezer."

"Outside," Felicia said, before Isabelle could answer. Felicia had strong opinions about temperature. She also, Isabelle had noticed, had strong opinions about which photos went on her social feed, and a person holding a trash bag in a parking lot photographed better than a person stacking cans under fluorescent light.

They worked the fence line for an hour, pulling plastic bags out of the chain link. Tyce showed up late with a printed sheet about service hours, which he needed for a scholarship application, forty of them by spring. He held the sheet while he gloved, then folded it into his back pocket with great care, as if the hours might wrinkle.

"This is three hours," he said, checking his phone. "I'm logging three."

"It's been one," Felicia said.

"Travel counts."

They argued about the epistemology of service hours, how you would even know how many you had, whether the number was something you counted or something a supervisor signed. Isabelle kept pulling bags. The fence kept producing them, one after another, like the ground itself was shedding. When the sun got high they went inside for water, and that was when she saw the poster.

It hung by the walk-in freezer, curling at one corner, and it was a history of the food bank itself, or of food banks generally. She read it while she drank. The world's first food bank was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, founded in 1967 by John van Hengel. She read the line twice. She had assumed food banks were old, church-old, porridge-and-bread old, and instead the whole idea was younger than her grandmother. One man in Phoenix had thought of it, and now there was this warehouse in her neighborhood, and ones in every city she could name.

"Interesting?" Felicia said, following her gaze.

"It says the first food bank ever was St. Mary's, in Phoenix, Arizona," Isabelle said. "Nineteen sixty-seven. A guy named John van Hengel started it."

"Boring. I thought it was a mug shot."

Mr. Gupta came through with a pallet jack and Isabelle asked him whether it was true, the poster, and he said it was, and that he'd been volunteering since he was younger than she was now, and he didn't stop, so she didn't get more than that from him, which she preferred. She could look it up later. She didn't like knowing things only from one poster on one wall.

She went back out with the last bag and stood by the dumpster thinking about it. Part of her wanted the whole thing to be older, to feel like charity was a fixed feature of the world, bedrock, something you could rely on without checking. The other part of her liked it better this way. If a man in Phoenix in 1967 had simply invented it, then the world wasn't arranged benevolently or malevolently, it was arranged barely at all, and people kept proposing things. She had spent most of the morning feeling like she was performing goodness for a photo, and now she felt like she was participating in an experiment somebody had started only sixty years ago and nobody had finished. She couldn't fully reconcile the two. She tried to compartmentalize them, the poster and the parking lot, the idea and the afternoon, and found they wouldn't stay separate. The bag in her hand was the poster, sort of. She didn't know how to say that without sounding like an essay.

Tyce was in the shade logging his hours, or negotiating them. The coach from the park district was saying travel didn't count. Tyce said the sheet didn't specify. Felicia was taking a picture of a full trash bag with the fence behind it, and she asked Isabelle to move left, into the light.

"In a second," Isabelle said.

She went back to the fence line instead. There was one bag left, high up, caught where the chain link met a post, and it took both hands and a jump, and it came down with a dry crackle, and inside it, when she balled it up, was a bird's nest, empty, woven through with a strip of blue plastic.

"Isabelle," Felicia called. "The light's going."

"One more minute," she said, and dropped the bag in the roll-off, and stood there holding the nest.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
The band room smelled of valve oil and the damp cork from somebody's reed, and Matthew sat in the last chair of the trumpet section holding an instrument he had owned for eleven days. He had bought it secondhand from a pawnshop near the highway, dented at the bell and cheap in a way he could feel in his hands, and he had told no one at school that he had never played before. His plan, if it could be called that, was to sit in the back, watch the fingers of the players in front of him, and fake it until the faking turned into something real.

Rogan, who sat two chairs ahead and had been playing since fifth grade, turned around before the downbeat. "You gonna touch the tuning slide this year or just look at it?"

"I'm warming up," Matthew said.

"You're holding your trumpet like it's a sandwich." Rogan said it without cruelty, the way you'd tell someone their shoe was untied, and turned back around.

The problem was not pride, exactly. The problem was that Matthew wanted two things at once and could not make them lie still together. He wanted to be good, which required admitting he was bad; and he wanted to belong in the room, which required seeming already good. Mr. Chowdhury, who ran the band, had a saying he'd pinned above the whiteboard: WE TUNE TO EACH OTHER. Matthew had read it every day for two weeks and understood it the way you understand a word in a language you don't speak.

Then came the Thursday rehearsal at the community center, the joint concert with the older players, the room with the folding chairs and the coffee urn in the corner. Mr. Chowdhury set his phone on the stand and opened the tuner app. "Tuning note," he called, and the room went quiet, sixty instruments waiting.

Khalid, who played clarinet next to Matthew's section, leaned over. "It's A above middle C," he said. "Four forty hertz. There's a whole standard for it, ISO 16. Some international group decided one note for the whole world."

"Decided a note?"

"Decided the number. Everyone everywhere tunes to the same A." Khalid shrugged. "You just match it and you're fine."

The oboe had a cold that night, so the app gave out the tone instead, a flat little buz that Matthew would later think of as the loneliest sound in music. The clarinets went first, then the flutes, then the saxes, each player bending toward the phone like the note was a candle flame. When it reached the trumpets, Rogan matched it in three seconds and Matthew, alone in the last chair, blew a note that was not the note.

Mr. Chowdhury looked up. "Again."

He blew it again. Closer. Still wrong. The older players in the community band, sagacious men and women who had been doing this longer than Matthew had been alive, did not laugh, which was somehow worse. One of them, a woman with gray in her braid, adjusted her own slide a hair and waited with him, as though his tuning were her problem too.

That was when Matthew understood something about the pinned-up saying, or thought he did. He had assumed tuning was private, a thing you did to yourself before the music started. But the phone on the stand was only the form of it. The note had a number, A at 440 hertz, fixed by a standard called ISO 16, and that number underpinned everything the room did together, but the number alone was not the point. The point was that sixty people agreed to lean toward one sound, and that a player who had chosen, eleven days earlier, to bluff his way into the room was now being tuned by the whole room's patience.

He pulled his tuning slide out a little, the way he had watched Rogan do it, and blew. Closer. He pulled it a hair more. The needle on Mr. Chowdhury's phone wavered and then centered, and the woman with the gray braid gave him a single nod, so small he might have invented it.

"Good," Mr. Chowdhury said, and raised his hands.

They played through the first piece badly, the brass rushing, the clarinets dragging, Matthew managing perhaps half the notes and none of them gracefully. He got lost in the middle section and stopped playing entirely for eight bars, moving his fingers over the valves in silence, faking it exactly as he had planned, except that now the faking had a direction. He was not pretending to be a player anymore. He was pretending to play, which was a different genus of lie, the temporary kind, the kind you use like scaffolding and take down later.

Afterward, while the chairs were being stacked, Rogan came over and stood beside him. "Your slide was way out. You know that, right?"

"Eleven days," Matthew said.

Rogan looked at him for a moment, then at the trumpet, then back. "Eleven days and you're within five cents of A. That took me a month." He picked up his case. "Monday, second lunch, band room. I'll show you the fingering for the solo part. You're going to want it before Mr. Chowdhury hears what you actually sound like."

"I actually sound like a dying goose."

"Okay," Rogan said, shouldering the case. "So we start with the goose."

Matthew laughed, slid his trumpet into its dented case, and clicked the latches shut.

activity: getting a first part-time job
story:
The movie theater smelled of butter substitute and carpet shampoo, and Connor sat across the desk from the manager in a small office behind the concession stand, filling out his first W-4. The pen was chained to a wooden block. Through the open door he could hear the ticket-taker greeting someone for the four o'clock showing, and the manager, who had introduced himself only as Rick, kept glancing at the popcorn machine as though it might escape.

"Seven twenty-five an hour," Rick said, tapping the top of the form. "Saturdays and Sundays to start, maybe a Thursday if you're good with the register."

Connor wrote the number on his hand while the manager checked the popcorn, because he wanted to remember it exactly, the way you remember a score or a street address. Seven twenty-five. It sounded small and official at the same time, like something carved somewhere in a building he would never enter.

He told Ellis and Precious about it that evening in the parking lot of the strip mall next door, where they sometimes sat on the concrete bumper behind the defunct frozen yogurt shop. Precious was eating leftover popcorn Connor had smuggled out in his jacket pocket, one kernel at a time, meditatively, like a person counting beads.

"Seven twenty-five?" Ellis said. "That's robbery. I make nine fifty at the multiplex in Fairdale." Fairdale was twenty minutes away, just over the state line, close enough that half their school district's families shopped there on weekends.

"Then your theater pays better," Connor said. "Big screens, fancier lobby."

"No, man, it's not the theater. My cousin said everyone over there makes more. Gas stations, grocery stores, all of it."

Precious held up a kernel and examined it. "Maybe the state is richer," she said. "They have that outlet mall."

That night Connor sat at the kitchen table with his mother's old laptop and typed the numbers into the search bar, not because he doubted Ellis exactly, but because the two figures could not both be normal and he wanted to know which one was. The first result said that the federal minimum wage had been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009. He read the date twice. It was older than some of the movies he'd be showing at work. So seven twenty-five wasn't Rick being stingy; it was a floor set by the whole country, and it hadn't moved since before Connor started middle school. But Ellis made nine fifty, and Ellis was not lying, and the second result explained the rest: many states and cities set a higher minimum of their own. Their state, apparently, had not. Fairdale, one line over, had. The same job, the same popcorn, the same Saturday nights, and twenty minutes of highway between them was worth two dollars and twenty-five cents an hour.

At school the next day he found Ellis by the lockers and showed him the screen. Ellis squinted at it, then grinned, then frowned. "So I've been denigrating your boss for nothing. I told Precious Rick was cheap."

"He is cheap," Connor said. "But he's cheap inside the law. It's the law that's stuck."

"Stuck since 2009," Ellis said. "That's before we could even ride a bike."

Precious had drifted over and was reading over Connor's shoulder. In her rhetoric class they had just started a unit on persuasion, and she liked to deploy the vocabulary on anyone who would hold still. "Okay, but what's your logos here? You're saying it's wrong because it's old? That's not an argument, that's just a vibe."

Connor started to answer, then stopped, because she was right, and he could feel the shape of how wrong his first answer would have been. Old wasn't the same as unjust. Plenty of old things were fine. But somewhere between the two numbers was a fact he couldn't get around: identical work, identical hours, and the border decided the pay. He believed in a country being one country, and he also believed Ellis deserved nine fifty, and those two beliefs were grinding against each other in a slow, tectonic way, the kind of shift you couldn't watch happen but could only notice afterward, standing in the changed landscape.

"It's not a vibe," he said finally. "It's that two people can do the same job and the line between states picks the winner. I don't know what the number should be. I just know it shouldn't be geography."

"Apply in Fairdale, then," Ellis said. "I'll get you the link."

Connor considered it honestly. The drive, the gas, the fact that Rick had already put him on the schedule and had a name tag made with his name spelled correctly, one r, two n's, which somehow mattered. And Fairdale's multiplex was a chain, all fluorescent and identical, while his theater had a balcony and a curtain that actually opened before the film.

"I'll think about it after my first paycheck," he said. "I want to see what seven twenty-five actually looks like when it's real."

Saturday, his first shift. He tore tickets for two hours, then Rick put him on the popcorn machine, and he learned that the kernels at the bottom burn if you walk away even once. When the lobby emptied out between shows, he stood at the counter with the scoop still warm in his hand and looked down the empty hallway at the lit rectangles of the auditorium doors. His name tag caught the heat lamp's glow. Outside, through the glass, he could see the road that ran toward the state line, ordinary and gray in the late afternoon, going exactly where he might decide to follow it.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
story:
Chase had agreed to spend the last week of summer at his grandfather's house partly because it had air conditioning and partly because his grandfather owned an actual wall of books, floor to ceiling, that smelled like pepper and old paper. The essay was due the first Friday of the semester. Ms. Zhao had assigned it in June with what Chase considered unnecessary cheer: a historiographical essay, she'd said, not on the French Revolution itself but on how historians had argued about it since 1800. "You're not judging the trial," she'd told the class on the last day. "You're watching the jury fight."

He'd understood roughly none of it in June. Now he sat cross-legged on the braided rug with four library books fanned around him like a dealt hand, his laptop open to a document titled Draft 2 (Real One This Time), and his grandfather's cat, Robespierre, kneading the nearest pillow with the serene violence of a small dictator.

"You've been staring at that page for an hour," his grandfather said from the doorway, holding two mugs. "In my day we called that thinking. Now I believe it's called buffering."

"I'm forming a thesis."

"Forming it out of what? Blank space?"

Chase turned the laptop so the old man could see. His draft began: The French Revolution has been interpreted many ways over two centuries, which raises the question of what an interpretation actually is.

His grandfather made a sound like a tire deflating. "That's not a thesis, that's a fog."

The essay had actually started, in a way, three weeks earlier, at the city history museum with Raquel and Leonidas, the last time all three of them were free before scattering. They'd wandered into a gallery of European history and stopped in front of a wall panel with a painting of a mob storming something. Beneath it, a brass-colored label read: 1789: The Bourgeois Revolution That Transformed France. Leonidas had squinted at it. "Bourgeois," he'd said. "Is that the museum's opinion or a fact?" Raquel had taken a photo of the label with her phone, the way she collected evidence for arguments she hadn't had yet. Chase had stood there feeling a small, specific itch, the kind you get when someone hands you a puzzle piece and you can see it belongs to a puzzle you haven't opened.

Now, at the rug, he texted Raquel: did you ever figure out that museum label. Her reply came in under a minute, which meant she'd been waiting: video call in 10, I have books, Leonidas is at his cousin's but he'll join.

When the call connected, Raquel was at her kitchen table with three books stacked like a wedding cake. "Okay," she said. "So the label is doing a thing. It states an interpretation like it's just what happened. It's quotation arbitrage, basically. You borrow somebody's claim and pretend it's the market price."

"That's not what arbitrage means, exactly," said Leonidas, whose face appeared in a small square, half in shadow.

"It's close enough and it's a good bit. Chase, you know whose reading that is? It's the Marxist one. Soboul. Albert Soboul, he's the big one. He argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class. That's the whole label, right there. Some curator agreed with him and didn't bother saying so."

Chase wrote it down. The itch from the museum, which had never fully gone away, suddenly had a shape: the label wasn't lying, but it wasn't neutral either, and the difference between those two things was the entire essay.

"That's one view though," Leonidas said. "My cousin's book says the revolutionaries were basically lawyers and journalists panicking, not a class rising up. Like a giant group project that went off the rails."

"A grandiose group project," Raquel said. "They rewrote the calendar. Imagine doing that for a school project. 'Also, October is now Brumaire.'"

"Point is," Leonidas said, "you've got Soboul saying class overthrow, and then other people saying political accident, and the museum just picks a side and sticks it on brass."

Chase looked at his fog of a first paragraph, then at the four library books, and began to see how the essay might actually go: not arguing that the Revolution was one thing, but showing how the answer kept changing depending on who was asking, and when, and why. Soboul writing in mid-century France was answering different questions than the nervous lawyers theory people were. The draft's new title, which he typed with some ceremony, was Whose Revolution? Two Centuries of Argument. He deleted Whose Revolution? after a minute, keeping only the second half, mostly to forestall Raquel, who would absolutely have said it sounded like a detective novel.

"Progress?" his grandfather asked, drifting through with a watering can.

"Some. I have to figure out what I actually think, though."

"Do you have to?"

"Ms. Zhao says a considered position. But I keep landing on, it depends, which feels like cheating."

"Is it a real depends," his grandfather asked, pausing at the bookshelf, "or a lazy one? There's a difference. A real one costs you something."

Chase thought about that while Robespierre migrated onto his knee. On the call the next morning, he tried the position out loud: that Soboul's class story explained something the accident story didn't, and the accident story explained something Soboul's didn't, and maybe the honest conclusion was that a revolution big enough to get its own calendar was probably big enough to be more than one kind of event at once. "But I can't prove that last part," he admitted. "It's just where I land."

"That's allowed," Raquel said. "Say it's where you land. Cite Soboul for his claim, cite the other guys for theirs, then say what stays open. Leonidas, tell him that's allowed."

"That's allowed," Leonidas said solemnly. "Also if you use the word 'synthesis' more than twice I'm coming over there."

Chase spent the last two afternoons at the dining table under the window, revising, the cat asleep on the pile of books he wasn't currently quoting. On Friday morning his grandfather read the final paragraph twice, set it down, and said, "I don't agree with all of it."

"Which part?"

"Haven't decided. Give me until the Revolution's bicentennial."

Chase laughed, closed the laptop, and slid the essay into his backpack between a graphing calculator and a half-eaten bag of pretzels, while Robespierre, unbothered by two centuries of unresolved argument, went on sleeping.

story:
The playground behind the rec center had one bench left in the shade, and Amelia had claimed it an hour before her interview, rehearsing answers she had written on index cards and then shuffled like a deck of losing hands. She was applying for the front desk job at the swimming pool, which meant she would have to look at strangers, greet them, and take their money, all activities she had spent eighteen years successfully avoiding. Her mother had driven her here partly out of kindness and partly, Amelia suspected, to propitiate the household gods after a week of arguments about tuition deposits, and had then wisely gone to sit in the car with the air conditioning and a magazine.

Farah arrived with two slushies, one blue and one an alarming red, and sat down on the swing beside the bench without swinging. "You look like you're waiting for a verdict," she said.

"I'm waiting for three o'clock. Tell me about yourself, Amelia."

"You go to Northfield, you volunteer at the animal shelter, you once organized a bake sale that raised four hundred dollars."

Amelia recited it and heard her own voice die at the end of every sentence, like a radio losing signal. Her eyes wanted the ground. There was a specific patch of wood chips near the slide she had studied so thoroughly she could have drawn it from memory, which was the problem: she could look at wood chips or she could look at a hiring manager, and apparently not both at once.

"Okay," Farah said, standing and draining the last of the blue slushie. "Come with me. There's a bathroom inside the rec center and it's empty, and I read about this thing last semester for psych."

The bathroom smelled of chlorine and lemon disinfectant. Farah demonstrated, feet apart, hands on hips, chin lifted, like a superhero pausing mid-flight over a city she intended to save. "Power poses," she said. "There was this study in 2010, claimed that standing like this raised your testosterone and lowered your cortisol. Like two minutes and your hormones actually changed."

Amelia tried it, facing the smear-covered mirror, and felt ridiculous and then, underneath the ridiculous, something like steadiness. "Did it hold up?"

"That's the thing. A bigger study in 2015 tried to replicate it and found no hormonal effect at all. The testosterone didn't move, the cortisol didn't move." Farah leaned against the sink. "But people still reported feeling more powerful. So it's not lying to your blood, it's lying to your head, and your head believes it."

Amelia held the pose and considered this. She had spent the summer reading about scientific method because Mr. Swampy, her old neighbor who tended a saturnine garden of failed tomatoes and stronger opinions, insisted that a claim and a replication were as different as a promise and its keeping. He had told her that over the fence in June, holding a watering can, and she had thought it was just another of his grumbles. Now she stood in a public bathroom dressed as her own action figure, and the replication had taken away the hormones but left the feeling, and she did not know which of those she actually needed for a job at a pool. Maybe the feeling was the whole medicine. Maybe the feeling was a placebo wearing a cape. She decided she could live with not knowing, as long as she could still look up.

"Rylee did this before her library interview," Farah said, checking her phone. "She stood in the stacks like Wonder Woman and got the job."

"Rylee also once fainted during a fire drill. Her evidence is mixed."

"Her evidence got her eleven dollars an hour."

At two fifty-eight, Amelia checked in at the front desk, and the manager, a broad woman with a lanyard and kind, tired eyes, led her to a folding table by the vending machines. "Tell me about yourself," the manager said, and Amelia looked up from the spot she'd chosen on the floor mat and kept looking, straight into the woman's face, and said she went to Northfield, volunteered at the animal shelter, and had once organized a bake sale that raised four hundred dollars, and this time the sentences ended like sentences instead of apologies.

When it was over, walking out through the playground toward her mother's car, Amelia caught sight of her reflection in the rec center's glass door, feet planted, shoulders back, hands nowhere near her hips. Farah was already texting, thumbs flying.

"So?" Farah's message read.

Amelia stood still in the doorway a moment longer, then typed back with two hands, chin up: "Ask me about myself."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
story:
Lily's mother had cleared the kitchen table of everything except her own laptop, where a deposition transcript glowed under her attention, and one space at the corner she kept free for Lily, the way she had since September. Lily set down her textbook, her notebook, and a mug of the peppermint tea her mother liked, which was not really an offering, since her mother had asked twice, but which Lily hoped would propitiate her into letting the overhead light stay on past eleven.

The problem was straightforward enough to be insulting until it wasn't. A farmer with forty meters of fencing wants a rectangular enclosure against a river, so only three sides need fence; find the dimensions that maximize the area. Lily had written the area as a function of width, had the whole polynomial sitting there in her notebook, A of w equals w times forty minus two w, and she knew the next step was something called the derivative, and she knew the derivative would tell her where the maximum lived, and she could not make herself believe it.

Brynn arrived at nine with her boots still laced and her own textbook under her arm, because their plan had been the library until the library closed early for a staff meeting. "Is your mom still working?" she asked at the door, lowering her voice before Lily could answer.

"She's on page two hundred of a deposition. Don't ask her anything until she asks us for tea."

"I heard that," her mother said from the kitchen, without turning.

Brynn sat in the free corner chair and opened her book to the same chapter. For a while there was only the sound of two pencils and the laptop's fan. Then Brynn leaned over and tapped the page where the textbook had printed, in a way that struck Lily as almost smug, the derivative of y with respect to x as a vertical fraction, dy over dx, numerator and denominator stacked like something you could cancel.

"Okay, this is the part I can't get past," Brynn said. "It's written like a fraction. Mrs. Chowdhury said it isn't one. Then why does it look like one? Why not just some symbol with a dot, like they do in physics?"

Lily had been circling the same question in the privacy of her own head for three days without admitting it. She flipped backward through the chapter, past the practice sets, to the historical note in a box she had skipped because boxes like that always seemed decorative. It was two sentences. She read them twice.

"It's Leibniz," she said. "The dy over dx notation comes from Gottfried Leibniz and it's still standard in mathematics today." She turned the book so Brynn could see, finger under the line. "So it's not that our textbook chose to write it like a fraction. It's inherited. Somebody wrote it that way three hundred years ago and everyone just kept doing it."

"That's either comforting or terrifying," Brynn said. "Like, they could have changed it and didn't?"

"Or it works. Maybe it works so well nobody needed to change it." Lily heard herself defending a notation she had resented ten minutes earlier, and the shift interested her more than the fencing problem. She copied the historical note into her margin, then wrote the farmer's area function again and took its derivative using the power rule, sliding the two down in front of the w the way the chapter showed, and the fraction dy over dx appeared at the side of her work like a signature she was finally allowed to use.

Then she set it equal to zero, because the chapter said a maximum sits where the slope flattens, and solved, and got ten. Width ten, length twenty, area two hundred. She checked it by brute arithmetic, trying nine and eleven, watching the area come up just short both times, and felt something in her chest unclench. It wasn't that the derivative had given her the answer. It was that the brute arithmetic and the calculus had agreed with each other, two witnesses telling the same story, and she trusted the answer more for having been found twice in two languages.

Her mother appeared behind them with the empty mug and looked at Lily's page. "You look like you won something."

"I found out why the book writes it like that," Lily said. "It's not random. It's Leibniz."

Her mother's face did its polite blankness. "I'm very happy for Leibniz," she said, and squeezed Lily's shoulder on her way to the kettle.

Brynn was quiet for a moment, erasing something. "But it still isn't really a fraction, right? Ms. Chowdhury said that too." She looked at Lily sideways. "So we're using a thing that looks like a fraction, works sometimes like one, isn't one, and we just inherit it."

"I think that's allowed," Lily said slowly, testing the idea even as she said it. "Like it's an embryonic version of something bigger that we haven't been shown yet, and the notation is pointing at it." She wasn't sure that was true. She wrote the two hundred square meters in a box anyway, and under the box she wrote the Leibniz fact again, small, as if filing it for later.

At eleven her mother turned off the overhead light from the switch by the doorway, leaving only the lamp over the table, and Brynn said, "Same time Thursday? I'll bring the graphing calculator," and Lily said, "Bring the one with the mark on it, mine eats batteries," and Brynn was already lacing her boots.

story:
The art shed at Camp Wenlock smelled of cedar shavings and turpentine, and its one window framed the lake so completely that Amy sometimes forgot to look at whatever Ms. Bakker had propped on the easel. Today the print was Frida Kahlo's self-portrait from 1940, the one with the thorn necklace and the hummingbird, and Amy had a worksheet due by dinner: colour, composition, symbolism, three paragraphs minimum. She had written two sentences and crossed out both.

"The bird's my favourite part," Enzo said, leaning over her shoulder. "It's just decoration, though. Like a pendant."

"It's not decoration," Amy said, though she could not yet say what it was, which was the problem. She could predicate an entire reading of the painting on that small dark body at the throat, or she could treat it as an accent of black against the green foliage behind, and the two approaches kept sliding apart every time she tried to hold them together. Ms. Bakker had said, on the first day, that a good critique names what it sees before it decides what it means. Amy had underlined that twice.

Chase sat cross-legged by the fan, saying the name aloud the way people argue about words. "Frieda. Freed-ah. FREEda." He was incurably impervious to correction, so nobody corrected him anymore; he simply liked the feel of the syllables, the phonetics of it, rolling the r sometimes and not others, as if the painting's author might hear him through the print and express an opinion.

The composition, at least, Amy could manage. Kahlo centred herself against dense leaves, animals flanking her shoulders, the monkey on the right and the black cat on the left, nearly symmetrical, so that the asymmetries pulled the eye: the thorn necklace cutting a diagonal, the bird dead centre at the throat, blood-dark, wings dropped. The palette ran cool and botanical except for that one warm insistence of skin. She wrote all of that down in her smallest handwriting, then stopped again at symbolism, because the worksheet wanted a claim and she had only a suspicion.

At lunch she carried her tray to the far table where a girl from Cabin Four sat alone, the one whose grandmother had visited on Family Day wearing embroidered blouses and selling no one anything, only talking. Amy had overheard a fragment then and been too shy to ask. Now she set down her tray and asked.

"Your grandma, the day she came, she said something about the hummingbird picture." The girl looked up, considered, then nodded like she had been waiting a week for someone to ask. "She said it's an old Mexican folk thing. My abuela kept one, a little dead hummingbird, on a string. She called it a charm. My mom hated it." Amy waited. "For luck," the girl said, spearing a tomato. "Luck in love. That's what she said it was for."

Amy walked back across the gravel with her lemonade untouched, holding the sentence the way she'd been taught to hold a loaded brush. In the shed she wrote: the dead hummingbird hanging at her throat is a Mexican folk charm for luck in love. Then she sat with it. Enzo, who had followed her in, read over her shoulder and made a low sound. "So it's not decoration," he said. "It's a wish." Amy said maybe, and meant it as a real answer, not a dodge. Because the charm might be sincere, a painter willing to bleed for love, or it might be bitter, a luck she doubted enough to wear thorns underneath it, and the painting would not tell her which. The monkey's grip on the thorns, the cat's flat stare, the closed mouth in the face of all that foliage, all of it could support either reading, and maybe the point was that Kahlo had built it so it could not be resolved from outside.

She wrote her third paragraph slowly, stating the uncertainty as part of the critique rather than around it, and when she finished, the light through the window had gone from white to gold on the lake. Ms. Bakker collected the worksheets without reading them yet, stacking them against her hip. Chase was still saying the name to himself, softly, "Free-dah," and Amy looked once more at the bird, its small dropped wings, the string the painter had almost not painted at all. "Luck in love," she said, to no one in particular, and capped her pen.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
story:
I had it handled, which was the thing nobody in that library seemed to believe. The assignment said to build a BankAccount class in Java with private fields and getter methods, and I'd written classes before, last semester, the one where Roman copied half my switch statements and we both got B-minuses. So when Jawad slid his chair toward my monitor and said I was doing it backwards, I told him I was doing it forwards, and everything after that was him catching up.

We were in the public library on Marsh Street because his apartment had no air conditioning and mine had a father who cogitated out loud about tuition while I was trying to type. Jawad had brought two iced coffees, and he set the second one by my elbow without asking, because he'd noticed I hadn't eaten, which I had also noticed and was ignoring. The plan was simple: write the class, write the getters, be done by four. He had a different plan, apparently, which involved me sitting there doing nothing.

"You haven't written a line," he said.

"I'm composing."

"You're stalling."

The truth, which I'm getting to, is that I didn't know how to start, and it was easier to look deliberate than lost. Jawad opened his own laptop, pushed it into the space between us, and typed a method called testGetBalance that asserted a new account should return zero. There was no BankAccount class. Nothing for the test to hold on to. He ran it and the whole thing collapsed in red, a wall of compile errors, and I laughed at him, genuinely, because he had just demonstrated that his code was worse than my nothing.

"That's the point," he said. "You start broken on purpose. Then you write just enough to turn it green."

"That's the stupidest order."

"It's called red, green, refactor," he said. "Kent Beck popularized it. Write a failing test, make it pass, then clean it up." He said it the way he said everything, flat, like he was reading a cereal box, which meant he'd read it somewhere and memorized it on the walk over. I told him writing the test first was like grading an exam before anyone took it, and he said no, it was like knowing what the exam was for before you wrote it, and neither of us won that round because neither of us could prove anything yet.

He nudged the keyboard toward me. Fine. I built the class, one private field for balance, a getter, a constructor. Ran his test. Green. I sat back and waited for applause, and instead he pointed at my getter and said the constructor name was misspelled and I had a stray semicolon after the method header that would bite me later. The refactor part, he said. Clean it up now that it passes. I wanted to argue that if it passed, it was done, but I'd said something like that twice already today and been wrong twice, so I fixed the semicolon, deleted a comment I'd written to feel busy, and added a deposit method with a guard against negative amounts, because I'd started to see how the test I hadn't written yet would think.

Ms. Tanaka came by somewhere in the middle of that. She's the librarian on Saturdays, the one who never shushes anyone but stands close enough that you shush yourself. She set a book beside Jawad's laptop, some thick genetics text he'd requested through interlibrary loan for a course he was testing out of, and she said, quietly, that his brother's remittance from the plant had cleared at her bank the day before, since their accounts were at the same branch, an odd detail she offered the way neighbours do. Jawad said thanks without looking up. She looked at my screen a moment longer, at the red test I was now writing for overdrafts, and said only, "That's a good color to see," and moved on toward the front desk, where a kid was trying to print forty pages of Minecraft skins.

I wrote a test that deposited a negative amount and expected an exception. Red. Then I made it pass. Green. Then I looked at what I'd built and moved the validation into its own method, because it was showing up twice, and Jawad nodded like I'd finally said something worth hearing. Three fields, five getters, a loop of red and green and clean, and by quarter to four the class was smaller than the version I would have written blind, and it worked, and I understood it in a way that felt like holding it rather than hoping about it.

What I still couldn't decide was whether the order mattered or just the discipline. Maybe if I'd written the class first and the tests after, I'd have arrived at the same file by four o'clock anyway. Jawad thought not. He thought the failing test was the part that made you honest, that you couldn't pretend you were done when the screen was still red. I thought that was a thing people say. But I hadn't written a single test I didn't have to, back when it was my choice, so maybe he was talking about me specifically and I was the evidence.

His phone buzzed. His brother's transfer, the second one this month, was delayed, and he closed the genetics book without opening it and started packing up. I copied my file twice, once to the drive and once to his, without asking, and slid the second iced coffee, half finished and sweating, back toward his side of the table. He picked it up, and Ms. Tanaka appeared at the shelf behind us with the hold slip still in her hand, and said, "You two know we close at five."

story:
The waiting room smelled of carpet cleaner and cold coffee, and Felix read the poster on the wall for the fourth time because there was nothing else to look at. It listed values, or principles, or whatever they called them, and one line had stuck with him since his first glance: Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit. He had written it on his palm in pen that morning, in case his nerves erased it.

Ms. Silva called him in. She was smaller than her voice, which came out saturnine and unhurried, as though she had already decided something about him and saw no reason to rush. "So. Campus delivery coordinator. Why you?" Felix told her about running the Yearbook distribution, about the spreadsheets he kept, about the time he stayed until nine re-sorting two hundred mislabelled parcels. He did not prevaricate, though he wanted to; when she asked about his worst failure, he admitted he had blamed the supplier for a week before admitting the order form had been his own mistake.

Then she slid a sheet across the desk. "Scenario. Your team votes to split deliveries between two pickup points instead of one central hub. You argued against it in the meeting. You lost. It's Thursday. The change goes live Monday. Your supervisor, who voted with you, is asking you how you want to handle the weekend. Write me your response. You have until five o'clock today to email it to the address on that page."

He walked out past a cashier restocking vending machine crisps, sat on a bench outside, and texted Hamzah. "Interview went okay I think but now there's a writing test due 5pm. Disagree and commit thing from that poster." Hamzah replied within minutes: "wait that's an actual amazon leadership principle. one of them. Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit. challenge the decision respectfully, then commit fully once it's made. my cousin works there, he says it all the time." Felix stared at the screen. His father would have said something about backbone too, except his father's version meant never yielding at all, which had cost him two jobs and most of his patrimony before Felix turned twelve. Two pickup points meant two sets of keys, two sign-off sheets, twice the chance of a lost package. One hub meant a bottleneck at noon. Both positions were defensible, and his father's way acknowledged only one kind of truth.

Dana was in the library café, and she read the scenario over his shoulder while he drafted. "So you tell the supervisor you still think it's wrong but you'll run it anyway," she said. "That's just caving." "It's not caving if you say why first," Felix said. "There's a difference between folding and committing after you've lost." Dana pulled the sheet toward herself. "Then show the difference. Write the disagreement like it's evidence, not a tantrum. Bullet the risks. Then write the commitment like you mean it, with dates." He typed while she watched, deleting his first two attempts, which were either apologetic mush or a lecture. The third one began: "Thank you for asking me directly. I want to be clear about where I stand before I describe how I'll support the change."

The email ran to four paragraphs. In the first he restated the decision fairly, without caricaturing it, because Dana had pointed out that a disagreement nobody could recognize was just noise. In the second he laid out the two risks he still believed were real: sign-off gaps between sites, and the noon bottleneck migrating rather than disappearing. In the third he proposed one safeguard, a shared log checked at eleven and at four, which they could adopt or refuse. In the fourth, he wrote the sentence he kept rewriting: "If the team keeps this decision, I will run both pickup points as though I had proposed them, and I will not relitigate it in the break room." He checked the clock. Four forty. He attached it, hovered, and sent.

He met Hamzah at the bus stop at five fifteen, and they did not talk about it much, because there was nothing to say yet. His phone buzzed twice on the ride home, once with a gym notification and once with a message from Ms. Silva: "Your log idea will be in the pilot plan. Interview results Friday."

Friday came as a slow morning and then a fast afternoon. At four o'clock exactly, the email arrived, three lines long, and Felix read it standing in the kitchen with the fridge door open. "Offer attached. Start in two weeks. Come in with that backbone and that log." He read it twice, forwarded it to Dana, and put the milk back. Then he sat down and opened the attachment, his father's face surfacing and receding somewhere behind his eyes, and began filling in his own name.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
story:
Christopher's mother handed him a folder before he even had his shoes on, the way she handed him things when she had already decided they were settled. Inside was a receipt for twenty prepaid driving lessons from a company called Open Road Alliance, purchased the night before at a booth in the hotel ballroom where she had gone for a craft fair. There were terms printed on the back in small type, a line for a signature that was already signed, hers, in her careful looping hand, and the phrase "all sales final" underlined twice in the original, as though underlining could make it more true.

"We got the premium package," she said. "There was a countdown on the screen. Ten minutes at that price."

At the driving school on Marsh Street, where Christopher had enrolled back in June with his own saved money, the instructor's desk was a landscape of forms. He signed a liability waiver acknowledging the school's cars, signed a consent form for the on-road portion, initialed the terms and conditions at the little tagged arrows. The clerk turned each page toward him like a card being dealt, and Christopher noticed how the signature did not end anything but began it: the small print said the signature meant he had read the terms, which he had not entirely, though he did now, waiting.

Marianne was there for her road test, flipping through her logbook. When he showed her the receipt, she read it twice. "This says the lessons are with certified instructors at participating locations. It doesn't say which locations. It doesn't say anything, basically. That sentence is tautological, it just repeats that lessons are lessons." She tapped the "all sales final" line. "My dad calls this the fine-print tax. You pay it when you don't read."

Shaylee, who wanted to be an accountant and said so without embarrassment, looked at it differently. "Twenty lessons at their booth price, and Marsh Street charges less per lesson for a twenty-pack. If you could sell what's left at the going rate, that spread would be arbitrage. Except you can't sell driving lessons, so it's just a loss." She said this the way other people said sorry.

Christopher's mother, when he called her that evening, began to remonstrate before he had finished his first sentence, saying she had signed, that a signature was a signature, that she had learned that much in fifty-two years. He let her run down like a clock. Then he read her the page he had found, printed from the library computer because she trusted paper. It was from the Federal Trade Commission, and it said buyers could cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations until midnight of the third business day after the sale. A hotel ballroom with a folding table and a countdown screen had to count as temporary, he thought, the way a tent counts as temporary even when it has a carpet in it.

He drove to the hotel the next afternoon on his learner's permit, his mother in the passenger seat with the folder on her knees, saying nothing, watching the road the way people watch the road when they are deciding whether to be angry. The booth was gone; the ballroom was set up for a wedding. A manager at the desk found a phone number, and Christopher called it in the lobby, holding the printed page flat against the marble while his mother stood beside him with her arms folded.

"Under the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule," he said to the voice that answered, "I can cancel this sale until midnight of the third business day." The voice put him on hold. A pianist somewhere behind the ballroom doors played the same four bars over and over, rehearsing. His mother looked at the receipt, then at him, and unfolded her arms.

The voice came back with an address for cancellation forms and a reference number, which Christopher wrote on the back of his mother's hand because it was the nearest paper. Two days later he was in the Marsh Street parking lot, keying his seatbelt, the cancellation already stamped and mailed, and Mr. Wong, the grey-haired instructor who smelled of coffee and pencil shavings, slid into the passenger seat and said, "Mirror, signal, shoulder check. Then show me what you've got."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
story:
Wyatt restocked the bruised apples in the produce aisle, turning each one so the soft side faced the back, and between apples he recited under his breath, "England, Portugal, cloth and wine." Ms. Francis had written those four words on the board Friday and then erased them before anyone had copied them down, and the exam was Monday. He had a shift until nine tonight and another tomorrow, and the study guide he'd made lived in his back pocket, folded so many times it had gone friable along the creases, threatening to come apart into quarters if he opened it once more.

Saige found him there, pushing a cart of clearance items with one hip. "She really did erase it," she said. "I asked her after and she just said, you were there, you should have listened." Saige had been two rows over when it happened, close enough to have heard the whole thing, which made her the only witness Wyatt knew of.

"I heard the book part," Wyatt said. "That it's from 1817. On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation." He shelved the last apple. "The rest went too fast."

The truth was messier than that, and he knew it while he said it. He had heard the whole explanation, every word, and then he had gone blank the way he went blank at whiteboards. In the flashback that visited him now, the one he couldn't stop replaying, he was standing at the front of the classroom with marker dust on his fingers and Ms. Francis asking, "So why would both countries gain, Wyatt, even if one of them is better at making both things?" and he had stood there for what felt like a full minute, long enough to hear the radiator tick, before saying "I don't know" in a voice he hadn't recognized as his own. Lyam, who sat by the window and never studied, had answered it in half a sentence. Something about what you give up. That was the part Wyatt wanted back.

"Break in ten," Saige said. "Quiz me on the food safety stuff and I'll help you with whatever you've got."

They took their break on the milk crates behind the store, splitting a bag of day-old rolls whose crusts had gone soft in the middle but crumbled dry at the edges. Saige read from the study guide about temperature zones and cross-contamination while Wyatt stacked empty pallets, and then she flipped his sheet over. "Okay. Ricardo. Tell me what you've got."

"David Ricardo," Wyatt said. "1817. The book is On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation. He set out comparative advantage with England and Portugal trading cloth and wine." He said it fast, the way you say a phone number before you forget it, and then slower, because fast wasn't the same as knowing. "So Portugal's better at wine and England's better at cloth. Or, I don't know, it doesn't even matter exactly which one's better at which. The point is they trade and both come out ahead. Both of them. Even if one country's better at making both things, which is the part I froze on."

"That's the part?" Saige asked, tearing her roll.

"That's the part I can't hold onto. Lyam said something about what you give up, and it made sense for about four seconds, and then it was gone."

Back inside, the store had its Saturday-evening rhythm, and Wyatt bagged while the cashier scanned. An older man came through with a cake whose corner had been crushed, the sponge friable where the box had buckled, and there was a small negotiation over whether the store or the distributor would indemnify the bakery for damaged deliveries, a conversation Wyatt overheard through the register's beep and the manager's folded hands, and which ended with the customer paying half.

Near closing, Lyam showed up. He wasn't scheduled, but he'd walked over from his house three blocks away to buy a gallon of milk for the morning and to stand around, which was what Lyam did. He leaned on the end of Wyatt's lane while Wyatt wiped the belt.

"You still torqued about Friday?" Lyam asked. "Because honestly, man, it's not that hard."

"Then explain it," Wyatt said. "Right now. If it's not that hard."

Lyam picked up a spare roll of receipt paper and turned it over in his hands. "It's not about who's best. It's about what you give up to make something. Ricardo's thing, England and Portugal, cloth and wine, that was the example. Portugal could be better at both and it still works out, because of what each side isn't making while it makes the other thing." He put the roll down. "I read ahead. Once."

Wyatt stood there with his rag going still on the belt. It wasn't a new fact, exactly. It was the same four-second thing from Friday, except now it sat still, because Lyam had said it standing next to milk crates and a crushed cake instead of from behind a desk, and because Wyatt had spent all day turning bruised apples so nobody saw the soft side.

"I get it," Wyatt said. "I actually get it."

"You said that Friday too," Lyam said, and grinned, and pushed his gallon of milk down the belt. "Ring me up. I only came in for this, I swear."

Wyatt reached for the milk, then stopped. "Wait. You're here, and you owe me for covering your shift last weekend."

"I don't owe you anything. You volunteered."

"Then cover mine tomorrow," Wyatt said. "You're better at bagging anyway, and faster. And I'm better at studying. Both of us come out ahead." He was already pulling his name off the schedule card. "Trade with me, Lyam."

Lyam laughed and set the milk down. "Fine, but you owe me one."

"Everyone owes everyone one," Wyatt said, and clipped the card back onto the board.
