activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
story:
The county library smelled of carpet glue and old paper, and Kate had claimed the corner table by the microfilm machine an hour before closing. Her laptop was open to an empty document titled, optimistically, "Thesis." The assignment was to write about the mill strike of 1934, the one her town commemorated every autumn with a wreath at the gate, and Ms. García had said only one thing about it in class: "Find out what the sources actually say, not what the plaque says." Kate had assumed that meant the sources would settle the matter. The sources, it turned out, could not even agree on whether the magistrate who called out the sheriff's deputies had acted to protect the strikers or to break them.

She had three folders now. The town's centennial booklet, published in 1984, described the magistrate as a peacekeeper. A 1935 union pamphlet called the same man a company tool. And a graduate thesis from 1972, which she'd found through the library's digitized archive, argued that both accounts relied on the same dozen letters and that the letters had been collected by people with reasons to collect those letters and not others. Kate read the thesis twice, then sat with her hands flat on the table. She had wanted a fact. What she had was a set of partial windows, each one facing a different direction.

Calvin dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of books he clearly wasn't going to read. "You look like someone stole your conclusion."

"Nobody wrote one." She turned the laptop toward him. "Every author was answering a different question. The centennial people wanted civic pride. The union wanted martyrs. The thesis guy wanted to know how memory gets made." She heard herself say it and realized it was the first clear thought she'd had all afternoon.

"So which one's true?"

"That's the thing. They're not lying. They're just, each of them only had pieces." She pulled the diary from her bag, the reason she'd come to the library in the first place, though the library's books had swallowed the original plan. Her grandfather's diary, 1934, kept when he was seventeen and apprenticed at the mill. Her mother had found it in a shoebox and said, "This'll settle it, he was there."

Calvin leafed through it, frowning. "There's nothing in here about the strike. Not one page."

"That's what my cousin Ilan said." Kate could still hear him at Sunday dinner, tapping the diary like a lawyer with evidence. "If it was such a big deal, he'd have written it down. Ilan says the whole wreath ceremony is inflated, that the strike was small and the town reified it into a legend because legends are good for tourism." She had almost believed him. Ilan was confident the way their grandfather was not, and confidence sounded a lot like proof.

She found her grandfather in the reading room the next afternoon, in his usual chair by the window with the large-print westerns. When she asked him about it, he laughed until he had to take off his glasses.

"An argument from silence," he said, still chuckling. "That's what my old teacher would've called that. You can't build a house out of what isn't there."

"But you didn't write about it," Kate said. "Ilan said that proves it didn't matter."

"Sweetheart, I was seventeen. I wrote down which girl I walked home from the dance with and how much a soda cost. The strike? That was just the weather, that week. Everybody knew about it, so nobody my age was writing it down for anybody." He put his glasses back on. "Ask me now, and I'll tell you about the deputies on the corner with their sticks, and the magistrate, and the night the windows went in at the company store. Ask me in 1934 and I'd have told you who I kissed on Saturday. Writers write down what seems important to them at the time. That's all a diary is."

Kate drove back to the library with his sentences running through her head, and she understood, slowly, that the historians in her folders had been arguing from silence too. The union pamphlet said the deputies were unprovoked because no company record mentioned giving orders; the centennial booklet said the strikers were peaceful because no arrest log listed charges. Absence, treated as evidence. She typed a paragraph, deleted it, typed it again. Her thesis, when it finally took shape, was not about who the magistrate really was. It was about how the answer to that question had changed every twenty years because the people asking it wanted different things from the answer, and about how the diary everyone thought would close the case had, in a way, opened it.

She kept the last page honest, the way Ms. García seemed to want: it was possible Ilan was right that the strike was smaller than the wreath implied, and it was possible the 1972 thesis writer had been too quick to distrust the union pamphlet. Kate could not resolve that from where she sat. What she could say was what the sources said, what they left out, and why the leaving out was itself part of the record.

At closing time, Calvin waved from the front desk where he was returning his unread books, and she packed the diary on top of the laptop. Outside, the streetlights were coming on along the road to the old mill gate. She stopped at the corner, took out her phone, and photographed the empty street where the deputies had stood, ninety years before, and where nothing now marked anything at all.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
story:
The town hall meeting had been called for seven, but by six forty the folding chairs were mostly full, and Christian stood at the back with his binder against his chest, flipping between two sets of notes he had labeled, in pencil, SCHOOL and STUDENT. His AP Government class was holding a mock Supreme Court next week, and Ms. Rahimi had assigned him the impossible version of it: argue both sides. Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., petitioner and respondent, one after the other, alone.

"You look like you're about to defend yourself at your own trial," Curtis said, sliding in beside him near the coffee urn.

"In a way I am." Christian turned the binder so Curtis could see. "Same case, two briefs. That's the assignment."

Rayne found them a moment later, still holding her car keys like she hadn't decided to stay. She had a reason to be here beyond the assignment; the school board was voting on a new social media conduct policy, and last spring she had been called into the principal's office over a Snapchat she'd posted from her couch on a Saturday, a photo of the parking lot with a caption she now described as "facetious, in retrospect, and also constitutionally interesting, if you ask me." Nobody had asked her, yet. That was partly why she'd spent a weekend researching and had texted Christian at one in the morning: the Supreme Court had actually decided this. She'd pasted the citation before he could answer.

The meeting opened with old business, a drainage easement, then the chair called the policy to the floor. When the board president read the proposed language, that the district could discipline students for online posts that disrupted the school environment regardless of where the posts were made, Christian felt the two halves of his binder press against each other through the cardboard. He raised his hand.

"I'm not speaking for or against," he said, once he reached the microphone, which felt like a facetious way to begin and he said it anyway. "I'm practicing. My class is arguing a real case next week. Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. In 2021 the Supreme Court ruled eight to one that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing her for an off-campus Snapchat post." He heard his own voice go flat in the way it did when he was reciting something he'd checked three times. "Eight to one. That's not a close call."

A man near the front, a parent Christian didn't know, said that was a different state, a different school, a different situation entirely.

"Maybe," Christian said. "That's actually what I keep trying to figure out." He looked down at his notes and found, to his surprise, that he didn't want them. "The hard part is that the school's side isn't stupid. If a post travels from someone's bedroom into a cafeteria fight, the school has to deal with the fight. And the student's side isn't stupid either, because if schools can punish anything we say off campus, there's basically no off campus." He paused, aware that the room had gone quieter than the drainage easement had gotten. "I can argue both. I've written both. I just can't tell you yet which one I actually believe, and I wanted to say that out loud somewhere public before I say it in a gymnasium in front of a scoreboard."

Someone laughed, not unkindly. The board president said the policy would be tabled for revisions, and the meeting shuffled toward cookies and disagreement. Ms. Rahimi, who had been sitting two rows in with her coat already on, caught him at the door and said only, "Come find me when you know which brief is the real one," and was gone before he could answer.

In the parking lot Rayne unlocked her car but didn't get in. "So which is it?"

"I keep trying to contextualize it," Christian said. "Your post, the cafeteria, the Court, tonight. Line them all up and see what connects." He looked back at the lit windows of the hall, where people were still standing in knots, arguing in low voices that carried anyway. "The thing I can't get past is entropy. Everything I read says the reason off-campus speech is different is that it can still cause a mess at school. Punishment spreads outward. Speech spreads inward. The two directions don't cancel out, they just overlap, and I don't know what the Court wanted us to do with the overlap."

"That's not an answer," Rayne said.

"I know. I'm being honest about it."

She leaned on the car door. Curtis, halfway to his truck, called back, "Argument's Tuesday, right? I'll be the one holding the sarcastic sign."

Christian zipped the binder into his backpack, both briefs still in it, and stood a moment longer watching the hall's windows go dark one by one as the last arguers were pushed gently out into the cold.

"Eight to one," he said, to nobody in particular, and started walking.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
story:
Lea's screen still showed zero rows, and she had checked the spelling three times. The query was supposed to list every customer who had never placed an order, and instead it insisted that no such customer existed, which Ms. Guo had promised was the whole point of the exercise. "You're looking for the people who ordered nothing," Ms. Guo had said at the start of the period, setting the tables up on the projector, "and the database will lie to you if you let it."

The lab was loud in the way it got near the end of the day, chairs scraping, someone's music leaking from earbuds. Nola leaned over from the next machine. "Mine works. Did you use NOT IN?"

"Yeah. Exactly like the board."

"Then yours works too. It's just an empty answer." Nola turned back to her own screen, and Lea stared at hers. An empty answer and no answer looked identical on the screen, and that was the problem, because she could not tell which one she was looking at.

She ran it again. Zero rows, again. She thought about the tables the way Ms. Guo had drawn them that morning, customers on the left, orders on the right, a line between them where a customer ID matched. Somewhere in the orders table, she remembered suddenly, one of the rows from yesterday's data entry had been saved with a blank customer. Esme had done it, and then spent ten minutes arguing that blank was a legitimate value because the form let her save it. The two of them had reached a kind of detente over it: Esme agreed to be more careful, and Lea agreed to stop hovering, and the row had stayed there, blank, in the middle of the data.

Lea deleted her WHERE clause and pulled up the raw orders instead, scrolling until she found it. There it was, the order with nothing in the customer column, sitting among the rest like it belonged. She counted the rows above and below it, then sat back and looked at the ceiling tiles for a second. Her query had been fine. She tested it, replacing NOT IN with a different join she half remembered from Tuesday, and this time names appeared, six of them, customers with no orders at all, printed neat and ordinary under the column header.

"Wait," she said to Nola. "Try putting a NULL in your subquery list. Like, actually run yours against a list with one NULL in it."

Nola typed, ran it, and frowned. "Nothing. Zero rows. But I just watched you find six customers."

"That's it. That's the trap." Lea turned her chair fully around. "If the list has even one NULL in it, the NOT IN returns no rows at all. Not fewer rows. None."

Esme had drifted over from the printer, arms crossed, the way she stood when she suspected she was about to be blamed for something. "One blank row does that?"

"One NULL anywhere in the list." Lea said it slowly, because she was still assembling it herself, the way the two facts fit against each other: the query was correct, the data was mostly correct, and together they produced a perfect silence. She had spent the period trusting the empty result, and the empty result had been a lie, and nothing had ever told her so.

Ms. Guo came by on her circuit of the lab and looked at Lea's screen without touching anything. "You found the six?"

"I found them. But I want to know why I got nothing before. I mean I know what happens, one NULL in the list and the whole thing returns no rows. I don't get why that's the design. Who decided empty should be able to eviscerate the entire answer?"

Ms. Guo's mouth moved slightly, not quite a smile. "That's the question for Thursday." She moved on to the next row of machines.

The bell hadn't rung yet. Lea copied her working query into her notes file, then, underneath it, typed the other one too, the one that had failed, with a single line after it: one NULL in the subquery's list, and it returns nothing at all. She didn't delete either version. On Thursday she intended to walk in with both, set them side by side on the projector, and ask Ms. Guo her question again until she got an answer. Esme was still standing there, watching the screen.

"So," Esme said, "should I fix the blank row?"

Lea looked at it a moment longer. "Leave it. For now."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
story:
Kevin's uncle had cornered him by the samosas again, the way he cornered everyone, and it took four minutes for the conversation to reach its inevitable destination. "So, debate champion, tell me. Is riba, interest, still haram when the bank is an app on my phone? The Quran never saw a smartphone." Kevin said something about context that even he did not believe, and his uncle laughed and moved on to the biryani, leaving Kevin with the uncomfortable feeling of having been disabused of his own confidence by a man holding a paper plate.

The regional tournament was in two days, and the motion was exactly this: whether an ancient religious rule could still bind people whose lives looked nothing like the world that produced it. Kevin had argued motions before, capital punishment, school uniforms, but those were easy, because he did not have to answer to anyone's grandmother afterward. His grandmother was at this gathering, three folding tables away, and she would hear about whatever he said. That changed the weight of every sentence.

He found Arwa by the tea urns, where she was guarding a cup with the vigilance of someone who had learned not to set drinks down near small cousins. She was on his debate team, and she had come to the hall because her own family was two streets away and she preferred his aunt's kheer. "I have nothing," Kevin told her. "I have quotes from both sides and they cancel out. Like matter and antimatter."

"Then stop collecting quotes," Arwa said. "Start collecting methods. How does anyone actually decide a thing the text never mentions? Your uncle asked about online banking. Somebody somewhere has ruled on online banking. Find out how."

There was a laptop in the hall office, an ancient thing the committee used for auction totals, and the imam's son, a taciturn engineering student who communicated mostly through nodding, let them use it after Kevin helped him carry a crate of paper plates. Kevin typed "online banking fatwa how" and braced for chaos. What he found instead was a single clean word, repeated across a dozen pages, like a door handle everywhere he grabbed.

It had reminded him of something, and the memory surfaced whole. Ms. Rahman, his eleventh grade world history teacher, once kept him after class because he had written that medieval scholars were "basically making things up." She had not raised her voice. She had asked him whether a judge making a ruling on a case with no precedent was making things up, or doing something harder, working carefully from what did exist. He had argued with her for ten minutes and lost, and had liked losing, which was a strange thing to notice about himself at sixteen.

Now he read, and Arwa read over his shoulder, and the word kept doing its work. One page quoted a scholar describing how rulings on car insurance, organ donation and cryptocurrencies had all been reached by the same route. "Ijtihad," Arwa read aloud, slowly, tasting it. "It says here it's the independent reasoning a qualified scholar uses to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts don't directly answer." She looked at Kevin. "That's your whole case. Both sides of your whole case."

"It's not an answer," Kevin said. "It's a way of answering. My uncle wants a yes or no and this is a maybe with a method attached." But even as he complained, he felt the problem rearranging itself under his hands. The motion asked whether the rule still applied. His affirmative case could argue that the reasoning tradition was itself designed for change, that a rule which travels through ijtihad is not trapped in the seventh century, it is carried forward, case by case. His negative case, the one he would have to argue if the coin went against him, was that this placed enormous power in the hands of whoever counted as qualified, and that reasonable scholars had reached opposite conclusions on the very same questions. Both were true. Both were arguable. He wrote fast, on the back of a dua schedule, while the engineering student watched with what might have been approval or might have been concern for the paper.

His uncle drifted back for a second samosa, or possibly a second round. "Figured it out, champion?" he asked. "Is my phone halal or not?"

"I think the honest answer is that the scholars are still reasoning it out, and that's not a weakness, that's the design," Kevin said. "There's a word for it. Ijtihad. The independent reasoning a qualified scholar uses to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts don't directly answer." His uncle chewed for a while, which for him was a long silence. "So the answer is homework," he said finally. "Wonderful. My religion assigns homework."

"Ours does too," Arwa said. "Yours is just kheer and blinking at people." The engineering student, passing with his crate, nodded once, and Kevin could not tell if the nod meant the joke landed or if the sagacity of the nod was simply beyond them all. He copied his notes into his phone, closed the old laptop, and went to find his grandmother before she left, to ask what she thought about the whole question, because she had lived through more versions of the modern world than either side of the tournament would ever cite.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
story:
The newspaper had arrived in Maelle's mailbox by accident, or so the sticker on the plastic sleeve suggested: addressed to her grandmother, three months after the funeral. She had carried it to the house anyway, up the porch steps and through the kitchen where the kettle still sat on the burner, because it seemed wrong to leave it in the car. On the table she smoothed the front page flat and understood, with a small cold drop in her stomach, why she had brought it. Ms. Hussain had told them, on the last day of the spring term, that first-year Arabic meant reading a real news article by September and summarising it aloud. Maelle had nodded then, the way one accedes to a demand that still feels theoretical. It did not feel theoretical now.

She could speak with the best of them. Eighteen years of Sundays at this table had given her that much, the dialect that lived in her grandmother's mouth and in the phone calls to cousins in three different countries. She read the headline slowly, sounding it out, and the letters assembled themselves into something almost familiar, the way a face is almost familiar across a crowded room. Almost. The words were not the words her grandmother used. She said one of them out loud, tentatively, and it sat wrong on her tongue, like furniture moved two inches in the dark.

She called Jaelyn, who had taken the same class and spent the summer in a different panic. "Does yours sound like yours?" Maelle asked, propping the phone against the sugar bowl. Jaelyn's copy was from her own library, a different paper, a different country on the masthead. She read the same kind of sentence aloud. It matched. Not the dialect, not any voice either of them had heard at home, but the same written shape in both papers, as if every newspaper in every region had quietly agreed on one way of writing while nobody told the people speaking at their kitchen tables.

"So it's not just us," Jaelyn said. "It's not that we learned it wrong."

"Then what did we learn?"

Jaelyn didn't answer, because there was nothing either of them could say that wouldn't sound like a betrayal of someone.

Maelle went back to the article itself. It was short, a piece about a bridge project, and she worked through it word by word with the dictionary app, marking the verbs. Here was something she could hold onto: a shared written language, one form serving readers in different regions, readers who would never speak to each other the same way but who could read the same page. It was like consanguinity, she thought, and then disliked the thought, because it was also unlike it. The newspapers were related by choice, by convention, not by blood. Her dialect was blood. She copied the third paragraph onto a notecard and began rehearsing the summary aloud to the empty kitchen, and her own voice in the empty kitchen made her stop.

Emmanuel had told her once, at the memorial, that their grandmother had read to him from the Koran when he was small, fluently, whole suras from memory. He had assumed she was reading. Maelle had assumed so too, all those years, and the assumption had been as evanescent as steam off the kettle, present and then gone, never once tested. She tested it now. She set the phone to record, dialled the number of a cousin in Amman, and asked her to read the bridge paragraph over the line. The cousin read it easily, unhurried, and Maelle followed the recording with her finger on the newsprint, matching sound to letter, and the written form that had felt like a locked door began, not to open exactly, but to show its keyhole.

But there was the other thing, the thing she had been circling all afternoon, and now she had to walk straight at it. If the papers were written one way and spoken another, then her grandmother, who spoke more beautifully than anyone Maelle had ever met, might not have been able to read them at all. The newspaper had come addressed to her name. It came every week, the mail carrier said when Maelle caught her at the box, had come for years, and someone must have subscribed it. Maelle stood at the mailbox with the carrier's engine idling and asked who. The carrier didn't know. Subscriptions, she said, were handled online now, mostly.

Inside, Maelle laid the paper on the table where it had always been folded, in thirds, spine toward the window, the way her grandmother had left every issue, and she understood that the folding told her nothing certain. Maybe her grandmother had read every word of every page. Maybe she had folded them unread, for the feel of the ritual, for the sound of the pages, for the company of them. Maelle would not ask Emmanuel, because Emmanuel would build a certainty out of either answer and she was not ready to watch him do it. She was learning, slowly, to hold two things at once: that her grandmother may have been excluded from this written form her whole life, and that she may have moved through it like a swimmer through water, and that no evidence Maelle had would ever choose between them.

She set up her phone on the sugar bowl, facing the chair where her grandmother used to sit, and began the summary aloud, in her rehearsed, careful, newspaper Arabic. Halfway through she stumbled on a verb, and without deciding to, she said it again the way her grandmother would have said it, the spoken word, the blood word, and let both versions stand there together in the quiet kitchen.

"Which one was right?" she asked the empty chair.

The kettle ticked as it cooled, and outside, the mail truck pulled away from the box.

Nevaeh sat in the driver's seat with her hands at ten and two, waiting while her mother walked around the car for the third time, checking tires as if the car might have changed since breakfast. The parking lot of the closed hardware store was empty except for a shopping cart marooned against a curb, and the rain had started as a fine mist that made the windshield look greased. Her mother opened the passenger door, folded herself in, and set a thermos between her feet like ballast.

"Mirrors first," her mother said. "Then go."

The engine sounded smaller from the driver's side. Nevaeh adjusted the mirror and saw her own eye, then the empty lot behind it, and eased out of the space with a caution that made the car barely roll. It had taken her two weeks to get here, two weeks of her mother saying Saturday and then Saturday meaning errands, and now that the day had finally arrived she wanted to be good at it immediately, which she understood was not how anything worked, and which changed nothing.

On the way out of the lot her phone buzzed in the cupholder. At the stop sign she glanced down. Marc: two seconds behind the car in front, that's all you need, I've been doing it since March, don't let your mom make you paranoid. She put the phone face down. Marc had forty hours of driving already and a kind of confidence that arrived before evidence, and she envied it the way you envy people who can fall asleep on any floor.

"Turn left here," her mother said. "There's no one coming. Take your time anyway."

The road was a quiet street of small houses, wet hedges, a man walking a dog under an umbrella. Nevaeh followed a silver hatchback and counted, because counting was the only instruction she had that felt like holding something. One. Two. She noticed the hatchback's brake lights, and the distance between them, and the rain thickening against the glass.

"Too close," her mother said, not sharply. "Marc tell you something different?"

"She said two seconds."

"Marc drives like the road owes her money." Her mother reached over and turned the wipers up one notch. "Look it up when we stop. Don't take my word."

They pulled into the lot of the library, and while her mother went in to return books, Nevaeh exhumed the driver's manual from the mess of napkins and registration papers in the glovebox, its cover bent, its pages soft with age, practically an antiquated document next to Marc's phone with its screenshots and its group chats. She found the section on following distance with her thumb already knowing roughly where it would be. The National Safety Council recommended at least three seconds, she read, and an added second for each difficulty, like rain or heavy traffic. She looked out at the wet lot, at her mother coming back down the library steps shielding the returned receipt with her hand, and did the arithmetic herself: three plus one for the rain. Four seconds. Marc's two wasn't just short of her mother's rule; it was half of what the day actually asked for.

On the drive home she practiced it. She picked a mailbox as the hatchback passed it, counted one-two-three-four before her own hood reached it, and felt the space open up around the car like a room getting bigger. It was strange to her that a number could do that. Her mother had said three and Marc had said two and both had spoken as though the answer lived inside them, when it turned out to live in a manual anyone could have read, and both of them had gotten it wrong in different directions. She wasn't sure yet which she trusted less, the overconfidence or the hand-me-down caution, and she suspected the honest answer was that she'd be finding out for years, in this car and others, on dry days and wet ones.

"Better," her mother said as they turned onto their street. "You felt that, right? The room you made."

"I felt it." Nevaeh slowed for the puddle at the corner where the storm drain clogged every winter, the one she'd been driven past a thousand times in the back seat, usually with Alia beside her, both of them half asleep, Alia the loyal acolyte of every driver who'd ever picked her up, always riding shotgun's shadow, always saying you're such a good driver to whoever held the wheel. Nevaeh had loved riding like that. She pulled into the driveway, set the brake, and sat for a second with her hands still at ten and two.

She picked up her phone and typed to Marc: found the actual rule, it's three minimum, plus one for rain, so today it's four. Then she deleted the last part, then typed it again, and sent it, and set the phone down on the dash while the wipers swept once more across the clearing glass.

story:
The library meeting room smelled of old carpet and someone's microwave soup, and Emma arrived early enough to claim the corner chair, the one with a view of the parking lot where the streetlights were just coming on. She had annotated her copy of The Great Gatsby with three colors of sticky notes, which she now regretted, because the notes looked like a shrine to a book she was supposed to be questioning.

"I finished it twice," said Muhammed, dropping into the seat across from her. He turned his copy over in his hands like a card he hadn't decided to play. "Second time I hated Nick more."

"Why?" Emma asked, though she had a theory, and though her theory had cost her two nights of sleep and an argument with herself she kept losing.

"Because the second time you see everything he doesn't say."

Mr. Ortiz, who ran the book club from the circulation desk on Tuesdays and the meeting room on Thursdays, wrote a single word on the whiteboard and then set the marker down: TRUST. "Before we begin," he said, "who do you trust in this room?"

"Ambush," muttered Maxim from the back, where he sat with his feet on a second chair and his copy still visibly unread, the spine uncracked. "That's an ambush question."

Mr. Ortiz only waited, which Emma had learned was his whole method, an patience that made you fill silences with things you hadn't meant to admit.

"I trust Nick at the beginning," she said. "And then I keep trusting him anyway, even after I catch him. That's what bothers me. It's like the wanting to trust him comes first and the reasons come after."

"That's how everybody reads," Muhammed said. "That's how everybody does everything."

"No, wait." Emma pulled her book toward her and found the page by feel, the way you find a bruise. "He says it outright. Near the end, after everything has already happened, after he's been to the parties and seen the wreck of it all. He says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.' That's the line. That's him telling us how to read him."

"And it's a lie," said Muhammed.

"It's not exactly a lie," Emma said, and heard herself hesitate, and heard the hesitation mean something. "That's what took me so long. I wanted him to be a liar so I could dismiss him, or honest so I could love him, and he won't sit still."

Maxim turned his chair around with a screech that made the man shelving large print flinch. "Give me one thing he actually hides. One. Because I read the SparkNotes on the bus here and I feel like a fraud."

Emma opened her notebook. She had made a list, and the list had become the argument, and the argument had become the thing she actually wanted to say out loud, more than she had wanted anything from a book before. "He tells us in the second chapter that he's drunk for only the second time in his life, at Myrtle's apartment, and then he narrates the whole ugly scene and skips what happened for the rest of the night. Wakes up in an elevator. He tells us he disapproves of Gatsby, everything Gatsby stands for, and then spends months as Gatsby's only real friend and arranges the meeting with Daisy behind Tom's back and never tells us what he thinks he's doing while he does it. He says Jordan is dishonest, and he's the one who ends it with her over the phone, sort of, and calls it a clean break when it isn't. And then the scathing part, the part that took me two readings to see. He leaves town and shakes Tom's hand and says Tom was a coward, and doesn't say a word about it to anyone until he's telling us."

The room had gone quiet in the way that meant people were checking their own copies, which was the sound of pages and the hum of the radiator and nothing else.

"So the narrator is doing the one thing he swears he never does," Muhammed said slowly, "and he's the one who tells us the sentence."

"And we believe the sentence anyway," Emma said. "Or half of it. I still half do. That's what I can't get past. Gatsby lies to everyone and Nick lies to us, but somehow we lionize Gatsby for it and forgive Nick for it, because Nick's the one holding the pen. Whoever's telling the story gets the last word and the first one."

"That's solipsism," said the woman from the Tuesday group, the one with the reading glasses on a chain, and Emma looked up, startled, because that was the word she'd been circling all week without landing on it. "If there's only the teller, no world outside his account of it."

"Or the opposite," Emma said. "The book keeps showing us a world outside his account. We keep catching it out of the corner of the eye. The green light. The parties. Jordan's little movements. It's all there whether he approves of it or not."

Mr. Ortiz erased the whiteboard, and Emma expected him to write something better, RESOLUTION or HONESTY, but he left it blank and capped the marker. "So who won?" he asked. "The teller or the world?"

"Nobody won," Emma said. "That's the point I keep trying to make and keep failing at. I want a rule I can carry to other books, a formula, and the formula keeps dissolving. Maybe you trust the narrator the way you trust a person. Not completely and not never. On a case by case basis, with your eyes open, knowing you'll be wrong sometimes and you won't find out which times until later."

"Which is exactly how it works with people," Muhammed said, "which is why the book's a hundred years old and still does this to us."

Maxim raised his unread copy like a toast. "To being wrong slowly."

Emma laughed, and started gathering her sticky notes back into their stack, three colors of certainty she no longer quite had. Outside, the parking lot had emptied except for one car with its headlights on and its driver still inside, engine running, going nowhere yet.

The email took Zoey eleven minutes to write and two seconds to regret. It had seemed clever at the time, a reply to Ms. Otieno's message about the yearbook proof deadlines: "Sure, I'll get right on that, since I obviously have nothing else to do senior spring." She had meant it as a joke between people who understood each other, the way she and Serenity joked in the margins of their calculus notes. But Ms. Otieno was new to sponsoring the yearbook, appointed only three weeks ago after the old sponsor's retirement, and her reply came back in four sentences, none of them warm. "I need a firm timeline by Friday. If the workload is unmanageable, we should discuss replacing you." No punctuation that softened it. Zoey read it three times at the long table in the library's back corner, where the afternoon light came through high windows and pooled on the laminate like something spilled.

"She thinks I'm mouthing off," Zoey said. Serenity sat across from her with a stack of flashcards, lemma written on half of them in blue ink, each followed by its careful proof. Abigayle had her boots up on a third chair and was peeling an orange in one unbroken spiral, a vestigial skill from summer camp counselor training, she claimed, though Zoey suspected she just liked the discipline of it.

"You were mouthing off," Abigayle said. "Just politely."

"That's the problem. It isn't polite on a screen. It reads like a door slamming." Zoey pulled the laptop closer. Somewhere behind them a printer chunked out page after page, patient as a heartbeat.

Serenity slid a flashcard aside. "So un-joke it. Write her a real one. Like an adult." She said "adult" the way people said a foreign word, testing it.

Zoey tried. The first draft began with three exclamation points and the word "totally," and she deleted it before finishing the sentence. The second draft was stiff as cardboard, all apology and no person. She sat back and stared at the ceiling tiles, wanting to understand the thing rather than just fix it, which was, Serenity had told her more than once, both her best and most inconvenient quality. It was inconvenient now, at 4:40 on a Tuesday, with Friday coming.

She found it in the school database while looking for something about business communication, which was itself a small surrender. A 2005 study by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues. Email writers, the study found, overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness. She read it twice, then read the line aloud to the table. "We think they can hear us. They can't." The words landed quietly among the flashcards and orange peel. She did not feel embarrassed so much as recalibrated, the way a map redraws a coastline you had imagined wrong. She had been so sure the joke would travel. It had not, and the certainty itself had been the error.

The email she finally sent was four short paragraphs. It stated the deadline she could meet, listed what remained for the senior section, and included one line of respectful disagreement: she thought cutting the club pages to two spreads was a mistake, and she said why, in order, with evidence, without hedging every claim into mush. She signed her full name. Then she closed the laptop and went to find Abigayle in the parking lot, because some things you stop introspecting about and just carry to the car.

Ms. Otieno replied the next morning, before homeroom. The reply was also four paragraphs, and Zoey recognized the structure the way you recognize a handshake offered back. The timeline was accepted. On the club pages, Ms. Otieno wrote that she had not known the photography club met weekly or that the robotics team had placed at regionals, and that Zoey should draft the four-spread version for the next meeting. The last line read, "Your first email was unclear. This one was not. I prefer this." Zoey read it standing at her locker, backpack still on one shoulder, and found she could not decide whether to feel insulted or promoted, and decided she was allowed not to decide.

At the Thursday meeting Ms. Otieno set two printed emails side by side on the table, the joke and the revision, and said nothing about either, only tapped the second one with two fingers and asked Zoey to walk the staff through the section budget. Serenity caught her eye across the room and mouthed lemma, holding up her flashcards like a toast. Zoey began with the fixed costs, the flexible costs, and the two assumptions she was least sure of.

"Those two," Ms. Otieno said, pointing, "tell me what to check first."

The summer Xavier turned sixteen, his mother left him at his grandfather's house every Tuesday while she took his grandmother to her appointments, and the Tuesday he brought his laptop, the old man pointed at it with his fork and said, "Put that away and play a game with me. Twenty questions. No, better, a number. I think of a whole number from one to a hundred, you guess it, I tell you higher or lower."

Xavier had homework open on the screen, a worksheet from the summer course he was taking at the community college, and the question he couldn't crack asked him to write, in plain English first and then in code, why one method of searching a sorted list beat another. He closed the laptop anyway. His grandfather had been a machinist for forty years and still judged people by their hands, and Xavier had learned that refusing a game was, in this house, a kind of rudeness that no grade could excuse.

He lost the first round in eleven guesses, wandering up and down the range like a man looking for a dropped ring in tall grass. His grandfather won the second round too, and the third, his acerbic commentary getting sharper with each victory. "You checked fifty-four and then thirty-one. Were you hoping the number would feel sorry for you and move?"

On the fourth round Xavier stopped guessing and started thinking. If the number was between one and a hundred, there was a guess that cut the whole range in half no matter what the answer was. Fifty. If the old man said higher, then a hundred numbers had become fifty; if lower, the same. Whatever came back, half of what remained died at once. He said fifty. Higher. Seventy-five. Higher. Eighty-eight. Lower. Eighty-two. Lower. Seventy-nine. Higher. Eighty-one. Six guesses, and his grandfather sat back in his chair like a man who had been shown a card trick he half remembered from childhood.

"Again," the old man said, and Xavier beat him in five. And again, in seven, the worst round yet, when the number turned out to be a hundred and he had to climb the whole ladder of halves to reach it. He kept a tally on the back of an envelope, because he did not entirely trust it, and the tally said that no round had gone past seven. Something in him wanted to test the edge of it, to find the number that would break the pattern, and nothing did. When his grandfather picked ninety-nine, it took seven guesses too, and Xavier wrote the number down and stared at it, feeling both that he had discovered something and that something had existed all along without him.

His phone buzzed on the table. Cade, from the course, had sent a photo of his own worksheet with the message "linear search is easier to write, why bother." Poppy had replied with a row of question marks. Xavier typed with his thumb while his grandfather shuffled the imaginary deck for another round: "if the list is sorted you can throw away half of it every step. Try to adjudicate which one you'd rather have with a million numbers." He read the sentence back and deleted "adjudicate," then put it back, because it was the right word even if Cade would mock him for it.

The grandfather's fourth loss in a row ended with him holding the envelope, squinting at the tally. "My grandfather played this with me," he said. "In Colombo. I never won a single round and I never worked out why." He tapped the paper where the seven was written twice. "You worked it out in an afternoon." There was pride in it, but Xavier heard something underneath the pride, a small door closing, and he understood that some games between them had just ended permanently, that the old man would not propose this one again.

When his mother came to collect him, Xavier opened the laptop in the hallway to finish the worksheet while the kitchen sounds carried on behind him. He typed the explanation he had promised, that a method going item by item through a sorted list touches everything it passes, while a method that always picked the middle of what remained never needed more than seven steps for a hundred things, and that in his code he would write the comparison, throw away half, and do it again. He was honest in the last sentence, too, because the worksheet asked what he was unsure of: he did not yet know what happened if the list was not sorted, or how to prove seven was the true ceiling rather than a lucky streak. Behind him, his grandfather said something acerbic to the radio. In class tomorrow, Cade would probably call the whole trick sophistry until he saw it run. Xavier saved the file, closed the laptop, and went back into the kitchen to lose at checkers.

The stadium smelled like ketchup and cold air, and Simon's grandfather had already told the story twice before kickoff. "I was there," he said, leaning across the nachos toward Axel and Aikam, who were sharing a blanket like it was a camping trip instead of section 212. "The very first one. January 15, 1967. Green Bay Packers, Kansas City Chiefs. Los Angeles. Thirty-five to ten." He spread his hands as if unveiling a monument. "I saw it with my own eyes."

Aikam, who had once spent an entire bus ride arguing that hot dogs were sandwiches, narrowed his eyes. "Weren't you born in 1961?" Simon knew this because his grandfather announced his age at every birthday like a scoreboard. He did the math on his glove, since his phone was buried under three layers. If Grandpa was born in 1961, then in January of 1967 he would have been five going on six. A kindergartner. In Los Angeles. Watching the first Super Bowl.

"Six," Grandpa said, undeterred. "Old enough to remember Bart Starr."

"You remember a game from when you were six?" Axel asked, with the delicate politeness of a boy who had been taught to respect elders and was failing beautifully.

"I remember the parking lot," Grandpa said. "I remember my father's hat."

Simon leaned back against the cold concrete and let the argument wash over him. He had spent the whole drive up trying to decide what he actually thought about family legends, whether they were lies or just stories wearing fancy clothes. His mother called them harmless. His uncle called them provenance, as if each disputed anecdote came with paperwork. Simon suspected the truth was sedimentary, laid down in layers: a real memory at the bottom, then a retelling, then a retelling of the retelling, until the fossil at the core was impossible to dig out without breaking something.

The teams took the field, and the crowd noise swallowed everything, so for a while there was only football. In the second quarter Simon found himself back in his grandmother's kitchen, eight years old, sitting on the counter while Grandpa recounted the Ice Bowl from 1967, the temperature so cold the whistle froze to the referee's lips. Simon had believed every word with his whole chest. He had drawn a picture of it for school: a gray field, tiny stick figures, a sun like a coin. Ms. Byrne, his teacher that year, had hung it on the wall and said Simon clearly came from a storytelling family. He had been proud of that for months. He was not sure he wanted to find out what the storytelling was worth, or what it cost.

At halftime, Aikam nudged him. "Just look it up," he whispered. "Settle it."

"He'll know I looked it up."

"He told us the score from memory, Simon. He wants to be checked."

That reframed things, the way Aikam's reframings annoyingly did. Simon dug out his phone, and there it was, exactly as advertised: the first Super Bowl, played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10, in Los Angeles. Every detail his grandfather had recited was correct. The date, the teams, the score, the city, all of it, remembered or carried or worn smooth by fifty-some years of retelling. It was the being there that wobbled, the claim underneath. Or maybe it didn't wobble at all. Maybe Grandpa's father had taken him. Maybe a six-year-old in a parking lot in Los Angeles remembered a hat forever, and everything after was just the layers piling up.

Simon looked up and watched the third quarter begin, the players small and bright and far away, like the stick figures he'd drawn at eight. He thought about how you could hold two things at once: that the story might not be true, and that it was still the truest thing his family owned. He couldn't prove either half. He decided he could live on that, like living on a field where you trust the ground without seeing the rock beneath.

He leaned over to his grandfather during a timeout. "The score's right," he said. "Everything you said checks out."

"Of course it does." Grandpa bit a nacho with tremendous dignity.

"But were you actually there?"

Grandpa looked at him for a long moment, then at the field, then at the scoreboard hanging above them all like a verdict. "Ask me again in fifty years," he said, "and I'll tell you whatever I remember." Then he stood up, cupped his hands around his mouth, and bellowed at the referees, "That was holding! I was six years old and even I could see it!"

The inflatable planetarium had been set up in the gymnasium since first period, a grey dome sweating under the basketball lights, and by the time Laurie's earth science class filed in after lunch the floor inside was warm enough that everyone kept their jackets on anyway, for the feeling of shelter. Ms. Fernando had them sit in rows on the mats and said only that they were there to look at atmospheres, then handed the clicker to whoever reached it first, which was Annabella.

Laurie had spent three evenings the week before with the carbon dioxide graph, the famous one, the sawtooth line crawling up the decades. She could read it now the way she could read sheet music, which is to say slowly and with her finger, and she wanted the field trip to make the numbers feel like something. In her notebook she had written a question she hadn't dared say out loud yet: are greenhouse gases a bad thing or a thing we depend on. It looked like a stupid question when written down. She kept it there anyway.

Annabella stabbed the clicker and the dome filled with stars, then with planets. "Do Mars," she said to Noemie, who was holding the guide sheet. "No, do the Moon." When the Moon came up, all craters and grey, a small line of figures appeared beside it, and Annabella read them out with the satisfaction of someone scoring a point. "Freezing. Boiling. No blanket." She turned around in the dark toward Laurie. "See, that's the Earth without greenhouse gases. Nothing."

"That's the Earth without an atmosphere at all," Noemie said. She was flipping through her biology flashcards on her knee even in the dark, mouthing genotype to herself, the instructions inside, as opposed to what actually shows up on the outside, and Laurie had the stray thought that carbon dioxide was a bit like that, invisible instructions the whole sky carried without showing anyone.

"Same thing," Annabella said.

"It's not the same thing." Noemie put the cards away. "My uncle does chemistry and he says without the natural greenhouse effect Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14. Fourteen is what we have now. With it."

Laurie felt the two halves of her notebook question click against each other. "So it's not that greenhouse gases are bad," she said slowly. "It's that there's a right amount and we went past it." She was working it out as she spoke, testing the floor with each footstep. "The graph I did, it's not measuring a villain, it's measuring an overdose. Same gases, wrong dose."

Annabella was quiet for a second, and in the planet glow Laurie could see her jaw set, which was unusual, because Annabella's opinions normally arrived at full volume and unbothered. "Fine," Annabella said. "Then the assignment should say that. It just says explain how greenhouse gases trap heat. It doesn't say write a love letter to them."

The subtext hung there in the dark the way the artificial stars did, slightly blurred. Laurie knew, though Annabella had never said it in class, that her father spent nine months a year on rigs, and that he had been home since spring, waiting on a phone call. Nobody mentioned it. Noemie rolled a flashcard between her fingers and looked at the Moon instead of at Annabella, and Laurie understood that they were all three of them deciding, wordlessly, what this conversation was actually about.

"Ms. Fernando would call that the parsimonious reading," Laurie offered, gentler now. "The simplest one that fits everything. Bad gases fits less. Gases plus amount fits more." She had learned the word in October and had been waiting weeks to use it in a sentence that earned its keep.

"It fits everything except my dad," Annabella said, and that was the first time she had said it, and she said it quietly, to the Moon.

Ms. Fernando's voice drifted over from the doorway of the dome, unhurried, telling them they had ten minutes, and asking, as if idly, whether anyone had managed to turn the graph into words yet, because numbers on a page had a way of pretending to be the thing itself, and a class that could reify a graph without explaining it had learned nothing. Laurie thought of the line she had traced with her finger, the small patient teeth of it sawing upward year after year, and how the graph made something enormous small enough to hold, which was a kindness and also a lie of scale, and she could not yet say which mattered more.

"There's still stuff I can't explain," she said to the dark between her friends. "Like why a little more of something the planet already needs tips the whole thing. I can read the graph and I can say the numbers, minus 18 without it, 14 with it, and the rest is still, I don't know, a shape I can see but not touch."

Annabella reached over and took the clicker back out of Noemie's hand. She advanced the dome to Earth, blue and cloud-swirled, and let it sit there, and after a moment she said, "Write that part down too. The part you can't touch. That's the part my dad would want read out loud."

The dome lights came up, stars folding away, and the mats were pale and ordinary again under them.

Her bill, the one she had drafted alone on her bedroom floor with three versions of the preamble crossed out, had survived its second reading by a single vote, and then committee, where Madalyn's amendments had carved it almost beyond recognition. Now it stood last on the orders of the day. Ms. McKenzie, supervising from the back row with a thermos, had told them only that the afternoon would test whether they understood what they had built.

"You realize what happens now," Roxane whispered from the bench beside her, leaning close under the cover of routine business. "Third reading. It's the final debate and vote on the bill as amended, after committee has gone through the details." Megan nodded, though her stomach tightened at the word amended. The bill she had brought to first reading proposed a small levy on the school's vending contract to fund breakfast programs. Committee had kept the levy but struck the breakfast programs, replacing them with a general student wellness fund, and Madalyn had done the striking.

There had been a night in November when Megan had gone to Madalyn's house to work on the amendment, the two of them cross-legged on the kitchen floor with the draft between them. "A wellness fund can instantiate the breakfast idea without naming it," Madalyn had argued, tapping the page. "Money for food, money for the nurse, money for whatever the school actually needs. Your version assumes you already know." Megan had liked the phrase then, the way it made her own clause sound small and presumptuous, and she had let the amendment through committee without a fight, telling herself that flexibility was the same thing as principle.

It was not the same thing, she was nearly sure of it now, listening to the Speaker read the bill's amended title aloud. Madalyn rose to speak first, gracious and precise, defending the fund's flexibility, and Megan found herself admiring the speech even as she disagreed with every polished sentence. A member from the government benches joked that the original breakfast clause had been a piece of epicurean social engineering, breakfast for all whether they wanted it or not, and the chamber laughed, and Megan did not, because hunger was not a peccadillo to be chuckled over, not in a school where she knew which kids took second helpings on Fridays.

When her turn came she stood, knees unsteady, and spoke to the amended text rather than against it, because the third reading voted on the bill as committee had left it, and there was no going back to her original wording now. "The fund is good," she said. "But a fund is a container. Breakfast is a commitment. I ask the house to consider what happens in September when the committee that disperses this money is new, and tired, and no one remembers why the levy existed." She sat down fast, her face hot, unsure whether she had argued for her bill or buried it.

The debate ran another twenty minutes. Roxane, who had been against the levy from the start, spoke surprisingly in favour, saying that Megan's clause had at least been honest about what it wanted, and that honesty deserved to survive. A boy from the third row proposed, hopefully, an oral amendment at the last minute, and the Speaker ruled it out of order, since the details had been examined in committee and the third reading was the final vote on what remained. Megan watched Madalyn take that ruling without expression.

They voted by standing division, and Megan stood with her own bill and counted heads while the tellers counted twice. Fourteen for, eleven against, and the Speaker declared the bill carried on third reading and reported it for the principal's assent, which everyone understood was a formality the staff took seriously in principle and loosely in practice. Madalyn crossed the aisle before the benches emptied and stood in front of Megan with her notes still rolled in one hand.

"I still think the fund is better policy," Madalyn said. "But your speech was the one that got it passed, so I'm not sure what I won." Megan looked down at her title page, the original crossed-out preamble still visible under her thumb where she had traced it during the vote. "Ask me in September," she said, "when we find out what the money buys."

story:
The licensing office smelled of floor wax and cold coffee, and Camille's grandfather claimed the only chair with a cushion while she took the number ticket from the dispenser. He had driven her the forty minutes into town himself, narrating the whole way, and in the parking lot he had gripped her wrist and said, "Remember, if anything happens, pump the brakes. Pump them. That's what kept me alive in the winters of '78." She had said yes because it seemed easier than saying anything else, and because he had taught her to fish and to shuffle cards and she owed him a certain loyalty in small things.

Reda and Maelys were already there, sprawled across the plastic chairs by the window with their temporary permits laid out like tarot cards. "You're with Marino," Reda said, nodding toward a woman in a gray windbreaker checking a clipboard. "She's fair. My brother said she doesn't equivocate about anything, which is either a compliment or a threat depending on how you drive." Maelys was chewing the corner of her permit and saying she didn't see why the road test couldn't just be a simulation, and Camille, watching the number display flip toward hers, said that a simulation wouldn't be the same because the fear would be optional, and fear was probably part of the data.

They argued about it lightly, Maelys claiming that was relativism, that if fear counted as data then everyone's driving was equally valid, and Camille trying to say no, that wasn't what she meant, some things were true regardless of who was frightened. Ms. Marino called her name before she could finish, and Camille stood, and her grandfather called after her, "Pump the brakes!" loud enough that three people looked up, and Ms. Marino's eyebrows moved a quarter inch.

The car was a white hatchback with a second set of pedals on the passenger side. Ms. Marino had her do the mirror checks twice, then a slow lap of the industrial estate behind the office, where the speed limit was thirty and the only hazards were parked vans. "Not bad," Ms. Marino said. "You listen. Most of them, I talk, it goes in one ear and out the other like weather." They merged onto the ring road, and Camille's hands settled lower on the wheel, and she found she could hold a lane without thinking about it, which was its own small astonishment.

It was Ms. Marino who raised the grandfather, not Camille. "The parking lot. Pump the brakes. Someone teach you that?" Camille admitted it, and waited to be told whether it was wrong. "That's the old way," Ms. Marino said, tapping the dash. "This car has anti-lock brakes. In a real emergency you press the brake firmly and hold it, and you can still steer while you do." Camille said, "Hold it? Not pump?" and Ms. Marino said, "Hold it. Steer." That was all, and Camille filed it next to the other version in her head, where the two of them sat like rival witnesses.

The problem was that her grandfather was not a liar, and the winters of '78 were not a fable. Both of them had given her instructions with the same certainty, and certainty, she was realizing, was not a guarantee of anything except itself. She was still turning this over when the cyclist came off the curb cut ahead, wrong lane, wobbling, a grocery bag swinging from the handlebar, and Camille felt her foot do what her grandfather had drilled into her, a quick stutter against the pedal, before she caught it. She pressed. She held. The pedal buzzed back at her like something alive and she did not lift her foot, and she steered, and the car slowed in a straight, shuddering line and stopped six feet short of the cyclist, who never looked up, who turned at the corner and pedaled away as if the whole event had been gratuitous, staged for no one.

"Good," Ms. Marino said, which was the longest word she had spoken in a minute. Camille's arms were shaking and she said so, and Ms. Marino said that was normal, pull in here. They sat in the forecourt of a shuttered garden center while Camille's pulse caught up with the rest of her.

Her grandfather had given her something true for a different machine in a different decade, and Ms. Marino had given her something true for this one, and Camille could not sort them into right and wrong, only into old and current, which felt less like a verdict and more like a debt she would keep paying. She did not know yet whether she would tell him, or whether telling him was a kindness or a small theft. Back at the office, Reda and Maelys were still in the window seats, and when Camille came in they both stood up at once, and she said, "I stopped for a cyclist," and Maelys said, "And?", and Camille held up her hands, which were steady again, and looked at them.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
story:
Alexis had dragged the folding table to the strip of shade beside the mailbox at nine in the morning, before the heat could calcify into the kind of afternoon that kept everybody indoors. The lemonade stand was technically her mother's idea, a way to occupy the last week before college orientation, but the economics textbook open on the corner of the table was entirely her own doing. She was on chapter three, comparative advantage, and she had read the same paragraph four times without it settling anywhere.

Jacoby arrived first, coastering his bike against the curb. He bought a cup, drained half of it standing, and leaned over the book. "Still doing that summer homework?"

"It's not homework if nobody assigned it," Alexis said. "I just want to actually understand it before September. Everyone acts like it's obvious and I don't think it is."

Ulysse came around the corner from the littoral road, the one that ran along the marsh where the river widened, his shirt salt-stiffened from helping his uncle pull crab traps. He set two quarters on the table. "Understand what?"

"Why trade makes both countries better off," Alexis said. "Not just one. Both. The book keeps saying it and I keep not believing it."

"Because it sounds like a trick," Jacoby said. "Like somebody has to lose."

"Right. That's exactly it." She poured his cup and watched him drink it, and the watching was what did it, oddly, or the drinking, because her eyes went to his hands, sunburned and rope-scraped, and then to the textbook's map of the world folded inside the back cover. Ulysse's family worked the water because the water was what this town had. The whole coast had it, miles of it, and almost nothing else.

"Okay, listen," she said, grabbing a napkin. "Say Ulysse's uncle is one country. He has, basically, a ridiculous amount of, I don't know, access to the bay. And say you're a country, Jacoby."

"I've always wanted to be a country."

"You have no bay at all, but you have that 3D printer in your garage and time on your hands. So you make things. He catches things. If he tried to build a printer out of boat parts it would take him a year, and if you tried to go catch crabs you'd drown."

"I would definitely drown," Jacoby agreed.

"So he trades crab for printers, and both of you end up with more crab and more printers than if you'd each tried to do everything yourselves. And it's not because he's better than you or you're better than him. It's because you're different. You have different stuff." She looked down at the napkin, where she had drawn a wobbly coastline and a garage, and felt something click into place, the way a jar lid does when you finally get the angle right.

Ms. Hussain from next door came out with her watering can and stopped at the table for her usual Friday cup. "Business steady?"

"Slow, but educationally rich," Alexis said, and told her the whole thing, the crab and the printer, both sides gaining. Ms. Hussain listened all the way through, which most adults didn't.

"Is that Heckscher-Ohlin?" Ms. Hussain asked.

Alexis flipped back through the chapter. There it was, in a box she must have skimmed past: the Heckscher-Ohlin model, named after the Swedish economists Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin, which explained comparative advantage by differences in countries' supplies of land, labor and capital. Not a trick, not a contest of virtue. Just differences in what places had to work with. She felt foolish for having missed it, and then less foolish, because she had walked to roughly the right place on her own.

"That's it exactly," she said. "It's literally called that."

"Sweden," Ulysse said. "Cold-water country. They'd have to trade for everything."

"Maybe that's why they thought of it." She wasn't sure that was true, and she said so. There were things she still couldn't answer, like what happened to the town's crabbers if the market turned, or whether a big country and a small one counted as equally free. She wrote those questions in the margin of the napkin, since the book's margins were too narrow.

Jacoby flipped the cup upside down on the table, empty. "So next Friday, same time, and I bring the printer stuff and he brings the crabs?"

"Bring both," Alexis said, and refilled Ms. Hussain's cup without being asked, free, the first trade of the day she had no reason to justify.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
story:
Hailey sat on her grandmother's porch with a legal pad balanced on her knees, the third draft of her ten-minute play crossed out in front of her, and decided the problem was not the writing. The problem was Adeline, who had read the draft over her shoulder at lunch and said, gently, that the fight between the two sisters felt borrowed, like something from a movie about writers writing plays.

"It happened," Hailey had told her. "That's the point. It's a moment from my own life."

"Then it shouldn't feel like somebody else's," Adeline said, and Hailey had carried the sentence around for two days like a stone in her shoe.

Her grandmother's house was where she always came to write, partly for the quiet and partly because the kitchen smelled of cardamom and nobody asked her questions until she wanted to answer them. Today her grandmother asked one anyway, setting down a mug of coffee Hailey was fairly sure she was too young to be offered. "What's the trouble?"

"Everything I put down about that night with my mom feels either too much or not enough. And there's a showcase on Friday, and everyone will see it, and if I hand my script to the printers tomorrow, some of those people could just take it." She heard how paranoid it sounded and said it anyway. "Kaila said a guy at her old camp had a whole script stolen before the showcase. Somebody copied it and put their own name on it."

Her grandmother dried her hands slowly on a dish towel. "And what would they do with it, do you think? Perform it in their basement forever?"

"Make it famous. Get into a program with it. I don't know."

Her grandmother looked at her the way she looked at a recipe she suspected of leaving something out, then went to the shelf where the dictionaries lived and pulled down a fat government-looking book with a spine like a doorstop. "Your grandfather bought this when he thought someone would steal his crossword puzzles. The government prints things you would not believe." She set it on the table and went back to the sink, leaving Hailey to it.

Hailey expected to find forms, fees, a waiting period. Instead she found a paragraph, plain as a bus schedule, stating that in the United States and many other countries a play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it is written down, without needing to be registered. She read it twice, then a third time, then carried the book to the sink and read it aloud to her grandmother, who said only, "Well, then," which was her way of saying she had suspected as much all along.

The relief lasted about an hour. Then it turned into a different question, sitting on the porch again with the legal pad, because if nobody could legally take the play, then the only thing protecting her from looking foolish at the showcase was the play itself, and the play was still borrowed feeling. She thought about what Kaila's story had really been doing, the story about the stolen script. It had given her a reason to delay finishing. She had been interpolating danger into the margins of every draft, little fears written between the lines, instead of fixing the lines.

She thought about Adeline's note, too, and about what Mr. Korhonen had said on the first day of the drama workshop, that a memoir scene fails when the writer protects the people in it. That had struck her as harsh until now. Now it seemed like a subtlety she had missed: the scene felt borrowed because she had kept the worst of it off the page, and what remained was generic, because the generic is what you get when you remove everything specific out of loyalty or fear.

So she wrote the fourth draft on the porch, and it was worse in one way and better in another. The worse part was that the mother in the play now said the thing her actual mother had said in the car that night, the line about how she wasn't sure she was the right parent for a kid like this, and Hailey's hands shook a little writing it. The better part was that the fight between the sisters, which she had originally staged as shouting, became instead the older sister going quiet in the passenger seat, and the younger one pretending to sleep in the back, and the affective weight of the whole scene moving into the silence instead of the noise. She could see it, suddenly, as a thing that could be staged. Two chairs and a steering wheel that didn't exist.

Her grandmother came out at dusk with two bowls of soup and asked how it was going. Hailey said she'd figured out the copyright thing, that she'd been worried about people stealing the script, and that it turned out the law covered it the moment she wrote it down, no registration, nothing to file. "I spent two days scared of something that was already handled," she said.

"Two days," her grandmother said, "is not so many. I spent a summer on the crossword thing." She tasted her soup. "And the scene with your mother. Is it fair to her?"

"I don't know," Hailey said. "That's the part I can't settle. It's true, and it's mine, and it might hurt her, and the law doesn't say anything about any of that."

Her grandmother considered this while the porch light came on, moths already circling it. "Then take her the script before Friday. Let her be an audience of one."

The next morning Hailey sat in the kitchen with her mother, who read the fourth draft without expression, and Hailey watched her hands on the pages and thought about how you can hold two things at once, the fear and the hope, and how neither one cancels the other. Her mother set the pages down and looked out the window for a long time.

"Read the sister's last line to me," her mother said. "Just that part."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
story:
The old First Regional bank sat at the corner of Marsh and Sixth with its drive-through lane still paved, and that was why Cyrus had chosen it. No traffic on Saturdays, a row of faded parking bays painted along the curb, and a mailbox just past the entrance that worked perfectly as a marker. Samantha eased her mother's sedan past the mailbox, reversed, cut the wheel, and tapped the curb hard enough to make her teeth click.

"You're at like forty degrees," Cyrus said from the passenger seat, feet braced against the floor. "You want thirty."

"Thank you, I could feel that." She pulled forward and started again, hands at ten and two the way the booklet insisted, though her mother drove with one wrist draped over the wheel like a woman absolved of every rule the day she turned thirty. Second attempt: closer, crooked. Third: crooked, farther. On the fourth she settled the car within a foot of the curb, straight enough that Cyrus clapped twice, which from him was a parade.

She had scheduled the test for the following Thursday, and between now and then lay the thing she actually feared, which was not parking but the highway. The examiner's route always included the on-ramp at Route 9, and merging made her hands sweat in a way no cone course ever had. Cyrus was stoic about most things, failed quizzes, his own expired license from a seizure disorder two years back, but he had opinions about merging. "My cousin counts," he said as she pulled out of the bank lot and pointed them toward the ramp. "She watches the car ahead of her pass a sign, then counts one-two-three out loud. Many driving courses teach keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead."

"One-two," she said. "But you said three."

"Three in bad weather. A longer gap in rain, snow, or darkness. It was raining when she took her test."

It was not raining now. The sky over the hardware store was the flat white of a sheet left too long on the line, and the on-ramp rose ahead of her like a dare. She checked the mirror, the blind spot, the mirror again. A silver pickup was climbing somewhere behind her; she could hear it more than see it. She held back instead of gunning it, watched the car in front of her pass a green mile marker, and counted, quietly, one. Two. Only at the top of the ramp, where the lane ended and became the road, did she press the accelerator and slide into a gap the size of a small argument. The pickup went by on her left, close enough that she felt the air move.

"Fine," Cyrus said, in a tone she chose to hear as impressed rather than noncommittal. "Do it again."

They did it again, and a third time, and by the third her counting had settled into the rhythm of the car itself, the way the steering had, the way the bank's curb had, mostly. She was beginning to understand that the two things she had been treating as separate fears, the precision of parking and the chaos of merging, were actually the same problem from opposite ends. Parking asked her to shrink her world down to inches and trust the wheel. Merging asked her to expand it to whole seconds and trust other drivers to be predictable. The test would demand both in the same twenty minutes, and she did not yet know which self she would be when the clipboard came out.

On Thursday it was raining. Not hard, but the real kind of rain, the kind that beaded on the windshield faster than the wipers' middle setting could clear it. The examiner, a heavy woman with a laminated sheet on her knee, directed her left out of the lot, and Samantha felt the old sweat start at the base of her thumbs. She drove past the bank, past the mailbox she had conquered a dozen times, and was told to park. She overcorrected once, adjusted, and came to rest nine inches from the curb, straight.

Then the highway. Rain streaked the windshield, taillights ahead of her ran together like wet paint, and she remembered what she had practiced and let the gap grow, watching the car ahead pass a reflective post and counting past two, into three, into four, holding the distance like something carried in both hands. The ramp was slick. The merge was ugly; she hesitated, a horn sounded somewhere behind, and she slid in anyway.

Back in the lot, the examiner made two marks on her sheet before she said anything. Samantha sat with the engine ticking and the rain soft on the roof, waiting to find out who she had turned out to be.

"Pull around front," the woman said finally, "and I'll show you where to sign."
