activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
story:
The line at the branch on Meridian Street had nine people in it, and Landon counted them twice, because counting was easier than rehearsing. On Monday his economics teacher had announced a contest: any student who could explain, to a bank employee, how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation would earn the last slot on the school's monetary policy team. Justin had signed up at lunch without looking at Landon, which stung more than the losing would, if Landon lost.

The bank smelled of carpet cleaner and warm paper. A guard held the door for a woman pushing a stroller, and the sound of the street, a bus sighing, a man on a phone, cut off each time the glass swung shut. Violet was already inside, sitting on the low bench by the pamphlet rack, wearing her debate-team blazer. She had beaten Landon in every argument they'd ever had since seventh grade.

"You came," she said.

"I came."

Justin arrived four minutes later, out of breath, collar damp. "They only have two loan officers free," he said. "So one of us waits."

They drew straws from the pamphlet rack, the thin paper kind that always tear. Violet pulled the short one. She straightened her blazer and walked to the counter, and Landon watched her lean in toward the teller, gesturing with both hands, her voice pitched just low enough that he couldn't steal her words.

Justin sat down beside him. He was quiet for a while, then said, "You remember the lemonade stand."

"Fourth grade. My driveway."

"You wanted to raise the price to a dollar because your mom said juice was going up." Justin turned a deposit slip over in his fingers, creasing it, uncreasing it. "I said no. I still think I was right."

"You were right about the customers. You were wrong about why." Landon had worked this out only last night, lying on his floor with the textbook open to a chapter he'd read four times. At the time he'd believed Justin was just being cheap. Now he could see the whole shape of it, the way you could see a constellation once somebody told you which stars to connect.

When Violet came back, her face gave nothing away. "The teller says the loan officer will see one more," she said. "The other one just went to lunch. So it's between you two." She looked at Landon. "Go. You've been mouthing the words since we sat down, and honestly, it's making me nervous."

The loan officer's desk had a nameplate, a jar of peppermints, a desk lamp with a green shade like something from an old movie. Landon sat across from her, and Ms. Whitaker, the nameplate said, folded her hands and said, "So. Convince me."

He started badly, saying the thing about borrowing costing more, then stopping, because everyone said that and it wasn't the part he cared about. He put his palms flat on the desk. "Can I back up?" he said. "There's this thing my teacher keeps saying, that expectations matter. Last night I thought it was just a phrase. Then I remembered a fight with my friend Justin." He told her about the lemonade stand, the dollar, the summer everything at the grocery store kept creeping upward. "We raised our price because we expected everything else to cost more next month. That's what a price increase is, a lot of the time. Not greed. Just people bracing."

Ms. Whitaker unwrapped a peppermint but didn't eat it.

"So here's what I think happens," Landon said. "If people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases. And that expectation itself helps keep inflation down. Raising rates is partly a bank proving it deserves that trust. It's expensive proof, and I can't actually tell you whether the proof is worth the cost, because my textbook has a whole page of economists disagreeing about it." He heard his own voice go thin on that last part, and he let it. "What I can tell you is that the fourth-grade version of me raised a price because of what I thought next month would look like. Multiply me by everyone."

Ms. Whitaker set the peppermint down. She asked him one question, whether he thought people's trust could be rebuilt once it broke, and he said he didn't know, and she wrote something on a card and slid it across the desk. His name, and a checkmark in green ink.

Outside, Justin was waiting with his bike helmet dangling from one hand. "Well?"

"I get the slot. But the part that mattered was ours. The lemonade." Landon looked back through the glass at the bench. Violet had her phone out, filming him, or pretending to. "Come on," he said. "I'll buy you a lemonade. Justin. A dollar."

story:
The cursor blinked at the top of an empty email, and Madison had forty minutes before the shop closed and Mr. Tanaka would expect the message in his inbox. She had taken the Saturday shift alone, and she had been the one who forgot to call the courier, and now a woman in Kelowna was going to walk into a conference on Monday without the thirty bound programs she had ordered for registration. The wrong was simple. The sentence describing it was not.

She typed a first line and deleted it. What she had written was "an error occurred in the processing of your order," which had the advantage of being true and the disadvantage of being a kind of fog. Nobody had done anything in that sentence. Things had merely happened, the way weather happens. She could hear Greta's voice already, the two of them arguing about this at lunch last spring, Greta insisting that distance was professional, that you never wrote "I screwed up" to a customer because it read like an overshare. Madison had half believed her then. She was no longer sure.

Her phone lit up on the desk beside the keyboard. Greta again, three texts in a row, sent from her own job at the pharmacy: "just say the delay was due to circumstances beyond our control. that's what we always do." Then: "no one wants your confession lol." Then a gif of a shrugging cartoon judge, which transfixed Madison for a second longer than it deserved, the little figure's shoulders rising and falling in an endless loop of indifference.

She pulled up the plain-language guide Mr. Tanaka had bookmarked on the shop computer months ago, back when he was rewriting the website. She had never opened it. Now she scrolled through the section on sentences and stopped where the guide recommended the active voice, in which the subject does the action, as in "I missed the deadline," because it makes clear who did what. She read the example twice. It was so plain it was almost embarrassing. I missed the deadline. Six words, no mist, and somewhere in them a person standing up.

The phone buzzed once more. Maci this time, who had taken the same customer-service training webinar at school: "whatever you write, don't do the 'mistakes were made' thing. our whole unit was basically about that." Madison smiled at the screen. Mistakes were made, passive voice like a blanket pulled over a body. She typed it into the draft just to see it there, and it looked exactly like what it was, a sentence designed to make the doer disappear.

But she didn't delete it right away, because Greta wasn't entirely wrong either. There was a version of candor that was really just a performance, all shame and trembling, that asked the customer to do the emotional labor of forgiving you. She wanted neither the fog nor the grovel. What she owed the woman in Kelowna was the facts, who had done what, and then the fix: she had reprinted the programs that afternoon, the courier would collect them at seven in the morning, and Mr. Tanaka had authorized a full refund of the rush fee, though the fee itself was ancillary next to the real cost, thirty people flipping through blank pages at a registration desk. That image, not her guilt, was the thing to answer for.

She wrote it straight through without stopping. "I missed the deadline for sending your order to the courier on Friday. Because of that, your programs will not arrive before your conference. I have reprinted the full order and it will ship tonight for delivery Tuesday." Then the refund, then her name, then the shop's. No varnish. She read it once, changed "will not arrive" to "will arrive Tuesday" in the second mention so the letter ended on the repair rather than the wreck, and sent it to Mr. Tanaka with the subject line reading "draft, need by 9." He replied in four minutes with a single line: "send it," and beneath that, unexpectedly, "I missed a courier deadline my first month here. 1998. The customer stayed with us eleven years." She sat with that for a moment, then sent the email to Kelowna herself, at 8:56.

The twist came on Monday. She was restocking the binding combs when Mr. Tanaka called her to the office and turned the monitor toward her. The customer's reply was already open, and the first line, which Madison had braced to find a travesty of an apology waiting for her in, read instead: "Thank you for saying plainly what happened. My last three suppliers would have written me a paragraph about circumstances." The rest of the message asked whether the shop could handle a standing order for next year's conference, four hundred copies, and whether the same person would be handling it. Mr. Tanaka looked at her over the monitor. "The same person," he said, "is asking for a raise, I hope." Madison laughed, and then didn't, because the woman had added one more line at the bottom, and it was that line she carried with her through the rest of the shift and onto the bus home: "I run a business too. The day I stopped hiding behind my sentences was the day my staff started telling me the truth." She looked out the window at the streetlights coming on, the houses sliding past, and wondered which she would be, at nineteen, at thirty, whether honesty was a thing you decided once or a thing you had to keep mailing out, one plain sentence at a time. Her phone buzzed in her pocket. Greta: "so what did you end up writing."

The resolution on the table read that the school should report students caught vaping to their parents, and Layla had argued against it for six minutes before she lost her place in her notes. She stood at the podium in Room 114 with the fluorescent light buzzing above her and thirty classmates watching, and she could not find the card that had her closing argument on it. Clark, seated in the second row for the affirmative, was trying to help without helping, mouthing something she couldn't read.

"Trade-offs," she said finally, giving up on the card. "That's what I keep coming back to. If we report kids to their parents, some of them get help. Some of them get thrown out of the house. We can't know in advance which, and the policy has to be written in advance." She heard her own voice steady down as she stopped performing and started thinking out loud, which Ms. Mansour always said was the moment to watch for in a debater.

Clark took the floor for rebuttal. "So Layla wants us to do nothing," he said, "because doing something might backfire. But responsibility means you accept the consequences of your choices. Her position is just fear with better vocabulary."

The room laughed, the small polite laugh of people who recognized a good line, and Layla felt her face go warm. She wrote Clark's sentence in her margin, though, because something in it bothered her, and the things that bothered her in debates usually turned out to be the interesting ones.

When the round ended and Ms. Mansour called for a ten-minute break, Naomi slid into the seat beside her. "You had it," Naomi said. "Then he made you sound like a dilettante, like you'd read one article and decided you were an ethicist."

"I did read one article," Layla admitted. "Two." She turned her phone over in her hands. "It's the Aristotle thing that's messing me up, honestly. Courage is a mean between two extremes. Cowardice and recklessness. So there's a version of telling on someone that's brave, and a version that's just reckless, and they can look identical from the outside."

Naomi frowned. "That's from your ethics book?"

"Nicomachean Ethics. Every virtue is a mean between two extremes, not just courage. So the question isn't whether to act, it's where the middle actually is." Layla glanced across the room to where Clark was reorganizing his cards, his nascent rivalry with her already famous among the freshmen, who had started coming to watch their rounds the way people watch weather. "Last month I told everyone in the group chat that he'd copied his physics lab. In front of everybody. I told myself it was brave."

Naomi was quiet for a second. "He still sits with us at lunch, so."

"Does he? He sits at the end. He moved his chair." Layla had been trying not to notice this, the way Clark had drifted to the edge of their table over the past weeks, and now the noticing felt like exhuming something she'd buried on purpose. "Maybe that's the cowardice-recklessness thing in real life. I wanted to be the person who says the hard thing. But I could have said it to him alone. I chose the version with an audience."

"You can't run the experiment twice," Naomi said. "That's the annoying part. You do the thing, or you don't, and you never get to see how the other version turned out."

Ms. Mansour leaned against the desk at the front and called the room back to order. "Second round," she said. "Same resolution, sides reversed. Layla and Clark, you'll be arguing each other's positions."

There was a ripple of amusement. Clark stood, gathered his cards, and crossed the room to trade stacks with her, and when he handed them over his eyes stayed on the floor. "Fair warning," he said. "I made you sound pretty reasonable in there. You're going to be good at this side."

She almost said it then, the apology or the question or whatever it was, but the timer was running and the room was waiting and the moment for quiet, private words had just been replaced by a public one, which was the whole problem to begin with. She stepped to the podium with his notes in her hand, his handwriting small and certain, and began to argue for the policy she'd spent the morning dismantling.

Somewhere in her second point she found herself saying that unintended consequences didn't absolve you of responsibility, they deepened it, because you were answerable for what you failed to foresee, and she watched Clark look up sharply as if she'd stolen something from him and was now showing it back. She didn't know yet where the middle was, or whether she'd ever find it, whether some people found it at all or only kept moving toward it. When the round ended, Clark was the first one standing, waiting for her at the front of the room with his hand out for his notes.

"We should get lunch," he said. "The end of the table, or wherever."

The kitchen smelled of star anise and scorched sugar, because their mother had been reducing the pork since noon and refused to admit the bottom of the pot had caught. Ethan sat at the counter with a stack of red envelopes, a ballpoint pen, and forty dollars in twenties that his father had handed him an hour ago with the instruction to make it look nice for the little cousins. On the stove, the braising liquid muttered. Down the hall, the vacuum droned in and out of rooms that were already clean.

His cousin Shiloh, fourteen and permanently hunched over a phone, had arrived early to help, which in practice meant sitting on a stool and narrating whatever appeared in the fridge. Now Shiloh slid off the stool, took one of the twenties, and smoothed it into an envelope with the seriousness of someone performing surgery. "For the little one," Shiloh said. "Mara. She's six, she won't even count it. She'll just chew on the envelope."

Ethan looked at the twenty, then at the second twenty still on the counter, and something shifted in his memory without surfacing fully. He had learned it somewhere, at some dinner, some overheard argument between an aunt and an uncle about what was proper. He cogitated on it, turning the bill over as though the fact were printed on the back. "Hold on," he said. "Don't put in forty."

"Why not? Forty's a good number. It's round."

"It's not about round." He set the bill down flat. "Red envelopes, money gifts, they avoid four. Any amount with four in it. The word for four sounds like the word for death, so you don't do it." He heard his own voice and worried it sounded like a lecture, but Shiloh only frowned at the envelope.

"Are you making that up?"

"I'm not making it up. Ask my mom."

Their mother emerged from the pantry with a jar of pickled radish and said, without being asked twice, "He's not making it up," and disappeared again. Shiloh pulled the twenty back out of the envelope and looked at it as if it had personally threatened someone.

The problem, then, was arithmetic. Ethan had forty dollars and three cousins under ten, and no way to divide forty that avoided the number entirely. He laid the bills out in a row and considered: two envelopes at twenty would spend it, but then Mara, the youngest, got nothing, and she was the one who actually chewed on things. Fifteen, fifteen, and ten meant going to the drawer for a ten he didn't have. He could go upstairs for his own money, the birthday money from his grandmother folded into the back of his wallet, and add it, but the whole point of red envelopes from him was that they came from him, and quietly subsidizing his father's generosity felt like a small fraud.

"It's not actually going to kill anyone," Shiloh said, watching him. "You could just put forty in and let it be."

"That's not how it works. It's not a superstition you can argue with, it's a politeness." Ethan wasn't entirely sure that was true either, whether the avoidance was dread or simply manners, like not giving someone a clock in another tradition he half remembered. He suspected different relatives would answer differently, and that he would never fully stand inside the knowledge the way his mother did. "It's like handing someone a gift that says death on it. Even if you don't believe in it, they have to look at it."

Shiloh was quiet for a moment, which was unusual. "Okay," Shiloh said, "then take one of the twenties back to your dad and put in thirty-eight for all three. Twelve, twelve, fourteen. Wait, fourteen has a four in it." Shiloh frowned at the ceiling, doing sums. "Twelve, thirteen, thirteen. None of those have a four. That's thirty-eight, and you keep two dollars."

"You're being facetious."

"I'm being practical. Two dollars is two dollars."

Their father wandered in for the tasting spoon, and Ethan slid one twenty across the counter to him without a word, then folded singles and a five from his own wallet into the gap. Ten, twelve, sixteen. None of them touched the number. He wrote the cousins' names on the envelopes in the careful characters his grandmother had drilled into him three summers ago, his strokes still slightly fat, like a child's, and set them by the door with the oranges.

Later, when the apartment had filled with aunts and the smell of the pork had forgiven itself, Ethan watched Mara tear open her envelope, ignore the money entirely, and put the red paper over her face like a mask. He still didn't know whether thirty-eight was generous or cheap, whether his mother's shrug earlier meant approval or surrender. But Mara marched across the room wearing the envelope, held it out to him, and said, "You're the dragon. Roar."

story:
Gabriella had been coaching the under-twelves for three weeks before she admitted, in the failing light of a Thursday practice, that nothing she did made any difference. The girls scrimmaged, they sprinted, they scrimmaged again, and every Friday they lost the same way, surrendering the ball in the middle third as though passing were a rumor someone had started and no one had confirmed. She stood at the edge of the field with her clipboard, its drills still inchoate, half-formed ideas about triangles and overlap that she could picture but not yet build, and she watched another square pass dribble tamely into a defender's feet.

She said none of this at home. What she kept to herself, what she turned over on the drive to Saturday games with her mother humming beside her, was that she had taken the coaching job for reasons she hadn't examined: the torn ligament in her knee had ended her own season in antiquity, as teenage time counted it, all of eight months ago, and coaching felt like the closest thing to playing that she was allowed. Ms. Kelly, who ran the recreation league, had handed her a whistle and a bag of pinnies and said the team was hers. Nobody had asked whether she knew what to do with them.

At school she found Silas in the library, spreading his history notes across a table like a man claiming territory. "You read everything," she said. "I need whatever psychology exists about getting better at things."

"You mean studying."

"I mean ten-year-olds who can't pass a soccer ball." She sat down across from him. "They play games all practice. Every practice, for weeks, since before me. Hours and hours. And they're exactly as bad as the day I met them."

Silas pulled a battered laptop toward him and typed, chewing his lip. Then he slid it across. She read slowly, twice. A study of violinists by K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues, from 1993. She read it a third time, her finger on the screen.

"Deliberate practice," she said aloud. "That's what they called it."

"That's what it's called," Silas said. "Effortful work on specific weaknesses, with immediate feedback. Not just logging hours." He reached over and turned the laptop back toward himself, protective as a dragon. "Which, if you'll notice, is the exact opposite of studying for the AP by rereading my notes, so thank you for ruining my afternoon."

She was already writing on the back of her hand.

Practice on Monday did not start with a scrimmage. She set up two lines of cones, five meters apart, and put a girl in each gap as a passive defender, and made the pairs pass around her, again and again, and every time a pass went astray Gabriella blew the whistle and said what she'd seen: hips closed, plant foot pointed at the sideline, eyes on the defender instead of the receiver. Immediate feedback, delivered in seconds. The girls groaned. One of them, the small fierce one named only in the roster as number nine, groaned loudest of all.

From the far goal, where he had been asked to shag balls and had instead been watching, Silas saw what Gabriella was too close to see. Number nine was the best passer on the team. Every ball she played in the drills was crisp and angled and correct, and she made it look like nothing, and Gabriella praised the strugglers and never once praised her. Number nine's shoulders had been climbing toward her ears for twenty minutes. What Silas understood, because he knew the want himself, the want to be the one somebody notices, was that this girl was not bored. She was starving. And a starving player quits, or worse, stays and stops trying, and then the whole inchoate machine Gabriella was building would lose its best gear.

He walked the balls over and set them down and said, quietly, "Nine's perfect. Say it out loud."

Gabriella looked at him, then at the girl, and understood that she had been so busy fixing weaknesses she had treated strength as a kind of scenery. She blew the whistle and called the group in and rearranged the drill: number nine at the center, two runners off her left and right, everyone else watching how she disguised her passes with her first touch. "Everyone gets a turn in the middle," Gabriella said. "Earn it."

By Wednesday the middle third belonged to them. On Friday they lost, two to one, but the first goal came from a pass number nine had slipped between two defenders without looking at it, and Gabriella, on the sideline with her knee aching in the cold, felt the whistle hanging cold against her sternum and did not blow it, not once, for the whole second half, just stood there watching the ball move the way she had always pictured it moving, waiting to see what happened next.

"Again," number nine said at the final whistle, to nobody, to everyone, already jogging back to center field.

story:
Kate had forty minutes before the library closed, and the essay she owed Mr. Joseph by eight a.m. was still an argument without a spine. She spread her books across the carrel by the window: two on the mill strike, one on the town's founding, and a photocopy of a page she'd taken from the reference shelf because the copy machine had eaten her quarters twice.

"You're the one who took the Carr," Montana said, dropping into the chair across from her. "I had it on hold."

"It's not checked out. It's reference." Kate turned the photocopy toward her. "I photocopied the page."

Montana read it, chewing the end of her pen. In his 1961 book What Is History?, E. H. Carr described history as "an unending dialogue between the present and the past." Montana tapped that line with the pen. "So which part are you? The present or the past?"

"Neither. I'm the essay." Kate pulled the strike book back. The problem was simple and she couldn't solve it: the two books on the mill strike, written thirty years apart, disagreed about why it failed. The older one blamed the organizers. The newer one blamed the police ledger that had come to light in the county archive, and the older book hadn't known the ledger existed. She'd written half a page in each direction and crossed out both.

Daxton arrived with his backpack still on and a printed schedule in his hand. "Library closes at nine tonight, not eight. I checked. You have more time than you think."

"I don't," Kate said. "I have to pick one. Mr. Joseph wants a position."

"Then pick the newer one. It has the ledger."

The closing bell for the second floor chimed, soft and pointless, a sound the library made at every hour. Montana leaned over and flipped the older book to its bibliography. "Look. He used the company newspaper and two interviews. That's all that was available to him."

"That doesn't make him wrong."

"It makes him incomplete," Daxton said.

"No, it makes his sources partial. Different thing." Kate heard herself say it and then had to sit with what she'd said, because she wasn't sure she believed it yet. If the sources were partial, then the question the historian asked decided what he found, and the questions came from when he lived. The 1961 book had said it better: a dialogue. The older strike book wasn't a wrong answer so much as one side of a conversation, the side that could be heard in 1974.

Montana was trying to parametrize it on the back of her schedule, drawing two axes. "One axis is what sources existed. One axis is what people wanted to know."

"That's too clean," Kate said. "The axes move each other."

"Then don't draw it like math."

Kate opened her notebook and started writing anyway, fast, because the clock above the circulation desk had started its slow climb toward nine. She wrote that the two books disagreed not because one author was careless but because the archive itself had changed between them, and because a historian in 1974 and a historian in 2004 had not been asking the same question of the same past. She wrote the phrase historiography, which she'd found in the index of the newer book, meaning the study of how histories get written, and then crossed out the definition because Mr. Joseph would know it and would mark it as padding.

Daxton read over her shoulder. "But you still have to say who's right. You can't hand in both."

"I can hand in a considered position," Kate said. "The newer account is more plausible. It's the parsimonious explanation, it needs fewer assumptions, and the ledger is primary evidence. But the first author wasn't stupid. He was answering the question his own decade asked." She stopped. "That's my position. That the disagreement is part of the discipline instead of a failure of it. And I can't prove the ledger settles it, because something else could surface in 2030 that makes both of them look partial."

"Mr. Joseph is going to say you dodged."

"Mr. Joseph is going to say I used evidence. If he wants a verdict, he can write his own essay."

Montana laughed and started gathering her pens. The floor lights dimmed twice, the signal the librarians used instead of announcements. Daxton zipped his backpack and waited while Kate photographed her notebook pages with her phone, in case the essay got lost between here and morning. At the door, the night librarian held it open and checked the carrel behind them for stray books. Kate went back for the Carr, returned it to the reference shelf face out, the way she'd found it, and tapped the cover once before following the others out into the parking lot.

"Eight a.m.," Daxton said. "Don't rewrite the whole thing at two in the morning."

"I'll rewrite the conclusion," Kate said. "It ends too neatly."

story:
The cultural center's main hall smelled of frying latkes and cold air let in through the lobby doors, and Anna stood at the long table near the window where the menorahs waited in a row. Her grandmother had been put in charge of the community lighting this year, which meant Anna had been put in charge of helping, which meant that at sundown, in eleven minutes, she would light the fourth-night candles in front of forty people who were counting on her to know what she was doing. The menorah in front of her was her grandmother's, silver and dented, and the box of candles beside it had been opened by somebody in a hurry.

"Fourth night," Haylee said at her elbow, craning to see. Haylee had come along because she liked any event with fried food and because her own family didn't do anything in December except argue about the thermostat. "So how many is that?"

"That's the problem," Anna said. She had set out five candles and then taken one away and then put two back, and now she couldn't remember which number she was defending. She counted the branches with her finger, lips moving, and stopped at the tallest one in the middle, set slightly apart from the others. Nine branches, but the ninth wasn't for a night, and for a moment she couldn't recall why she knew that, only that her grandmother had said it once in the kitchen, years ago, while wiping the silver with a cloth.

"That one's the shamash," said Amar, who had drifted over from the sign-in table where he'd been handing out programs. He pointed at the middle branch. "The helper candle. It lights all the others." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, as though information were something he was passing across a table rather than announcing, and then he went back to stacking programs because he was Amar and did not linger where he wasn't needed.

Anna looked at the row of branches and let the arrangement settle in her mind the way a sentence settles when you finally hear its grammar. Eight branches for the eight nights, one more candle each night, and the ninth branch holding the one candle that did the lighting and was never counted among the eight. Tonight, then: four candles for four nights, and the shamash, separate, taller, first. She set them out slowly, counting aloud under her breath, and the shape of the mistake she'd almost made felt smaller now, almost funny.

"You were one short," she told Haylee, holding up the fourth night candle. "I almost was too."

"Looks the same to me either way," Haylee said, with a sardonic lift of her eyebrow toward the crowd gathering near the stage. "They're all going to burn down to nothing in like an hour."

Ms. Wanjiru, who ran the center and had approved the Hanukkah event along with the Diwali display in the west corridor and the posada in the gym, came by to check the matches. She had a way of standing beside a person that made the room feel organized without anyone having been told what to do. "Sundown in six minutes," she said, not as a warning but as a fact she trusted Anna to use. She touched the edge of the white tablecloth, straightened it a centimeter, and moved on. Anna watched her pause at the far end of the hall to help an old man find the chair nearest the radiators, and something about it steadied her, the way the whole building was being held up tonight by a hundred small acts nobody would report.

The crowd hushed in the way crowds do when the last of the daylight goes. Anna's grandmother stood beside her, hands folded, and Anna struck the match and lit the shamash first, the helper, and then, shielding the flame with her palm, carried it along the row to the newest candle and back through the other three. The blessings her grandmother sang were in a language Anna half knew, and she hummed where she couldn't follow, and the light doubled itself in the dark window glass so that there seemed to be two menorahs, one inside and one out in the street, both burning.

Afterward there were latkes and the thin sweet jelly doughnuts, and Haylee appeared at her side again holding a paper plate stacked like a strategic reserve. "Your grandmother is telling everyone you did it from memory," Haylee said. "No pressure for next year."

Anna laughed, but the pressure was already there, a small stone in her shoe. She had almost gotten it wrong. Four candles, five candles, the shamash miscounted as a night, and the whole room would have watched the error burn all evening, serene and bright, a mistake with a veneer of tradition over it. She found herself standing next to her grandmother near the coat rack, wanting to confess the near-miss, and found that she couldn't decide whether to frame it as a failure or as the thing that had taught her. Both felt true. She thought of how Ms. Wanjiru moved through the hall, and how Amar passed facts like salt across a table, and how her grandmother trusted her without asking whether trust was earned yet, and she decided, provisionally, the way you decide most things at sixteen, that she would keep all three ways in her pocket and see which one fit tomorrow.

"Can we do five tomorrow night?" asked a small boy tugging her sleeve, the old man's grandson, apple sauce on his chin. "Not the candles. The doughnuts. Five doughnuts."

"One more each night," Anna said, crouching to his level. "I think that's the rule." She wasn't entirely sure the rule extended to doughnuts, but she said it with confidence, and he nodded solemnly, as though a precedent had been set.

From across the hall, her grandmother caught her eye and raised the shamash candle she was carrying back to the table, the one she'd saved from the box to replace the stub still smoking in its holder.

story:
The deadline was Sunday midnight, and by Friday afternoon Isabella still had eleven empty bars. She had spread her staff paper across her grandmother's dining table, where the light came through the lace curtains and fell in pale stripes over the treble clef she'd drawn four times before getting it right. The assignment, handed down by Mr. Moretti at the start of the week, was a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes written in standard notation, and she had managed five bars that didn't embarrass her.

Her grandmother moved through the room with a watering can, humming. She hummed while she watered the ivy, hummed while she straightened the photographs on the sideboard, and the humming resolved itself, as it always did, into a hymn. Isabella had heard the hymn a hundred times without hearing it. Now, with pencil stopped mid-stem on an F sharp, she heard the last two chords pass under her grandmother's breath, and something in her mind stood up.

"Wait," she said. "Do that again. The end."

Her grandmother turned, watering can suspended. "The end of what, dear?"

"The last bit. What you just sang."

Her grandmother sang it again, the final word of the hymn, the Amen, and Isabella wrote the two chords as fast as her pencil could move. IV to I. She had copied that progression off the board in theory class on Tuesday without it meaning anything, and here it was in her grandmother's kitchen voice, as ordinary as the smell of the ivy. She remembered Mr. Moretti saying the name while she was half-asleep over her notes: the plagal cadence, the Amen cadence, because so many hymns sang Amen to it. She found the phrase in her notebook now, circled twice, and realized she had heard the name without ever once hearing the sound.

"You look like you've found money," her grandmother said.

"It's called the Amen cadence," Isabella said. "That's what it is. That thing you just did."

Her grandmother laughed and went back to the ivy, and Isabella sat with her pencil hovering. Her problem had never been the first five bars; it was the ending, which kept landing on a perfect cadence, V to I, so final it felt like a door slamming. She had wanted something softer for the last phrase, and now she had it, though a doubt arrived with it: a plagal ending might not sound finished to Mr. Moretti at all. It might sound like she'd simply stopped.

She texted Joanna, who had finished her own melody on Thursday and had been facetious about it ever since, claiming she'd written the piece of the century in a single evening.

"Question," Isabella typed. "If I end my sixteen bars plagal, IV to I, no V anywhere near the end, is that a real ending or a cop out?"

The reply came in three bursts. First a thumbs up, as if Joanna were adjudicating the matter on Isabella's behalf. Then: "Hymns end that way all the time." Then, a minute later: "Hymns have words tho. The Amen is the words. You've just got notes."

That was the trouble, laid out flat. Her grandmother's cadence carried its certainty partly in the word it held; Isabella's melody would have to carry it alone, in the weight of the chords beneath the final phrase. She thought of Louis-Philippe, who had argued in class that a piece should always end the way a sentence ends, with the harmony leaning forward into the resolution. He'd want the V. He had said, leaning back in his chair, that anything softer was an apology.

There had been a détente between them since the winter, when they'd fought over the jazz arrangement for the winter concert and hadn't spoken for a month. She'd been the one to end it, showing up at his locker with a printed copy of the chart, every one of his suggested changes crossed out except two. He'd laughed. They'd been careful with each other since, friendly but formal, and she didn't want to text him now and reopen the question of who knew better about endings.

But she did anyway. "Plagal ending on the theory project," she wrote. "Yes or no. One word."

He wrote back a single word: "Coward."

She put the phone face down on the table. Two years ago, at this same table, her grandfather had sat across from her while she struggled through her first piano book, and he had said that a melody should end the way Sunday ended, quietly, with the sense that everything would begin again. He had died in the spring, and the piano sat against the far wall with a doily on it, and the watering can her grandmother carried was the same one he used to carry, and the hymn her grandmother hummed was the one he used to hum, which meant her grandmother was still humming to him, in a way, and the Amen was still landing where he could hear it.

Isabella worked through the afternoon. She filled bars six through eleven with a phrase that rose and hesitated, then spent the last four bars letting the harmony settle, IV to I under the final held note, no V, no apology. She notated it in pencil first, then ink, and checked every stem and every accidental twice. It didn't feel like Louis-Philippe's slammed door. It felt like the lace curtains letting the light through.

At the kitchen doorway her grandmother paused with the empty watering can.

"Play it for me," she said. "The end part. I want to hear my Amen."

The radiator in Marcus's truck had died on the highway outside town, which was how he found himself at the counter of Mr. Ramos's coffee shop, counting quarters for a medium drip and hoping the bus schedule he'd photographed on his phone was still accurate. Behind him, Rania and Eloic argued in the low, urgent way of people who have been arguing for days.

"The car is mine half the week," Eloic was saying. "My father's insurance, my father's rules."

"Half the week is not half the driving," Rania said. She spread a sheet of paper across the table, a grid in three colors. "You have it Monday, Tuesday, Thursday. I get Wednesday and Friday and both weekend mornings. That's not a schedule, that's a tax."

Marcus carried his cup over and sat down without being invited, because after eleven years of school with these two he had stopped waiting for invitations. Rania slid the paper toward him. They were all starting at the same college in September, all living at home, all needing the one car Eloic's family was willing to share, and the grid was their third attempt at fairness in as many nights.

"Look at Saturday," Rania said. "I have the lab job at eight. Eloic has nothing until his shift at two."

"So she wants my Saturday mornings," Eloic said, "and she's calling it fairness."

Marcus studied the grid. He had spent the spring in Mr. Ramos's economics elective, a class he'd taken only because the guidance counselor said it fit the empty block, and one idea from it had stuck to him the way certain songs do. He traced the columns with his finger, checking who gained and who lost under each swap. There was one move, he thought, where nobody lost: Rania took Saturday morning, and in exchange Eloic took her Thursday evening, which she'd admitted she hated because it broke up her study night, and which he'd admitted he wanted because his Thursday class let out at six. One person better off, actually two, and no one worse off.

"There's a name for that," Marcus said. "A Pareto improvement. Named after an economist called Vilfredo Pareto. It's a change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off."

Eloic looked at him over the rim of his cup. "And the Thursday thing?"

"Would be one. If you actually want Thursday evening."

For a moment the argument seemed to be resolving itself, and Marcus felt the small vanity of having found the hinge. Then Rania's pen stopped moving. She didn't look up. "I didn't tell you everything about Thursday," she said, and the pace of the room changed, the milk steamer suddenly very loud behind the counter. "Thursday evenings I drive my grandmother to her dialysis. I said I hated the drive because I hate saying the real reason. I don't want it in the grid. I don't want it discussed."

Eloic sat back. Marcus understood, slowly and with a sour feeling, that the elegant swap he'd constructed had been built on information that was friable, that crumbled the moment anyone leaned on it, and that Rania had let them argue for three nights over colors and columns partly to keep this one cell blank. The heuristic he'd carried out of Mr. Ramos's class, this tidy test of winners and losers, presumed that people put their losses on the table. Rania hadn't. Whether that was dishonest or simply hers to withhold, he couldn't decide, and he noticed that deciding felt less urgent than it had five minutes ago.

"You could have just said there was a Thursday problem," Eloic said, but quietly, and without the old edge.

"You could have asked why I was fighting so hard for a morning you don't even use," Rania said.

Mr. Ramos came around the counter with a cloth and wiped the table next to theirs, unhurried, as though the three of them were weather. Marcus thought about how the class had valorized efficiency, had held up arrangements where nobody lost as though losing were the only cost worth measuring. But here was a trade that made everyone better off on paper and would have made Rania worse off in the one way she had refused to write down. Maybe every perfect grid sat on top of something unwritten. He didn't say that out loud, because saying it would be another kind of leaning.

"Take Saturday mornings," Rania said finally, capping her pen. "All of them. I'll tell my lab I can't open. And Thursday stays mine, no reasons given."

"That's not a Pareto improvement," Eloic said. "You're worse off."

"I'm worse off in the grid," Rania said, folding the paper into quarters and putting it in her pocket. "The grid doesn't get everything."

Marcus turned his cup in its saucer, the handle making a slow circle, and outside a bus went past with the Saturday route number lit in its window.
